Surat al-Ahzab is Madinan, according to all of them. It was revealed concerning the hypocrites and their harming the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), their slandering of him, his marriages, and other matters. It has seventy-three verses. This surah used to be equal in length to Surat al-Baqarah. It also contained the verse of stoning: "The elderly man and the elderly woman, if they commit adultery, stone them absolutely as a punishment from Allah, and Allah is Mighty and Wise." Abu Bakr al-Anbari related this from Ubayy ibn Ka'b. The scholars interpret this to mean that Allah lifted from al-Ahzab what exceeds what is in our hands, and that the wording of the verse of stoning was lifted. Ahmad ibn al-Haytham ibn Khalid related to us, saying: Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Maryam related to us from Ibn Lahi'a, from Abu al-Aswad, from 'Urwa, from 'A'isha, who said: "Surat al-Ahzab used to equal two hundred verses during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When the Mushaf was compiled, only what is now there could be ascertained from it."

Abu Bakr said: The meaning of this statement of the Mother of the Believers 'A'isha is that Allah lifted from Surat al-Ahzab what exceeds what we have. I say: This is one of the aspects of naskh (abrogation), and the discussion of it has already been covered fully in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 2, p. 61 onward.]], all praise be to Allah.

Zirr narrated, saying: Ubayy ibn Ka'b said to me: "How many verses do you count in Surat al-Ahzab?" I said: "Seventy-three verses." He said: "By Him by whom Ubayy ibn Ka'b swears, it used to equal Surat al-Baqarah or be longer. We recited from it the verse of stoning: 'The elderly man and the elderly woman, if they commit adultery, stone them absolutely as a punishment from Allah, and Allah is Mighty and Wise.'" Ubayy meant that this was among what was abrogated from the Qur'an.

As for what is reported, that this addition was in a sheet in 'A'isha's house which a domestic animal ate, it is the fabrication of the heretics (al-malahida) and the Rafidites (al-rawafid).

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O Prophet, fear Allah, and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ (33:1)

His Exalted saying: ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah﴾. The particle "ayyu" (أَيُّ) is vowelled with a damma because it is a vocative of a singular noun, and the attention-drawing particle (al-tanbih) is obligatory with it. "Al-nabiyyu" (النَّبِيُّ) is an epithet (na't) of "ayyu" according to the grammarians, except al-Akhfash, who says it is a complement (sila) of "ayyu." Makki said: "Nothing is known in the speech of the Arabs of a single noun serving as a complement to something." Al-Nahhas said: "This is an error according to most grammarians, because a complement is only ever a clause. What can be argued in its favour is that, since it is a necessary epithet, it was called a complement, just as the Kufans call the epithet of an indefinite noun a complement to it." It is not permissible to put it in the accusative on the position (of the vocative) according to most grammarians. Al-Mazini permitted it, treating it like your saying: "Ya Zayd al-zarif" (O Zayd, the witty one), with "al-zarif" in the accusative on the position of "Zayd." Makki said: "This is an epithet that can be dispensed with, whereas the epithet of 'ayyu' cannot be dispensed with, so putting it in the accusative on the position is not good. Also, the epithet of 'ayyu' is in meaning the one addressed, so its accusative is not good."

It is related that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) migrated to Madina, and he loved the conversion of the Jews, namely the Banu Qurayza, al-Nadir and Banu Qaynuqa', and some of them had pledged allegiance to him while concealing hypocrisy, he would be gentle towards them, honour their young and old, overlook any ugly conduct from them, and listen to them. Then this was revealed. It was also said, as mentioned by al-Wahidi, al-Qushayri, al-Tha'labi, al-Mawardi and others, that it was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, 'Ikrima ibn Abi Jahl, and Abu al-A'war 'Amr [in the originals: 'Umar] ibn Sufyan, who came to Madina to stay with 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, the leader of the hypocrites, after Uhud, and the Prophet (ﷺ) had granted them safe conduct so they could speak with him. 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh and Tu'ma ibn Ubayriq stood with them and said to the Prophet (ﷺ), while 'Umar ibn al-Khattab was with him: "Abandon mention of our gods, al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat, and say that they have intercession and protection [in Asbab al-nuzul: benefit] for whoever worships them, and we will leave you and your Lord." This grieved the Prophet (ﷺ) greatly. 'Umar said: "O Messenger of Allah, permit me to kill them." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed I have granted them safe conduct." 'Umar said: "Get out, under the curse and wrath of Allah!" So the Prophet (ﷺ) was ordered to expel them from Madina, and the verse was revealed. ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah﴾ means: fear Allah.

﴿And do not obey the disbelievers﴾ from the people of Makka, meaning Abu Sufyan, Abu al-A'war and 'Ikrima.

﴿And the hypocrites﴾ from the people of Madina, meaning 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, Tu'ma, and 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh, in what you have been forbidden from, and do not incline towards them.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing﴾ of their disbelief, ﴿Wise﴾ in what He does to them. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is related that Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, 'Ikrima ibn Abi Jahl, and Abu al-A'war al-Sulami came to the Prophet (ﷺ) during the truce that existed between him and them, and 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, Mu'attib ibn Qushayr and al-Jadd ibn Qays stood with them, and they said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Abandon mention of our gods." He related the report with the same meaning as the previous one, and that the verse was revealed concerning the breaking of the covenant and the annulment of the truce. ﴿And do not obey the disbelievers﴾ from the people of Makka. ﴿And the hypocrites﴾ from the people of Madina in what they asked of you. It is related that the people of Makka invited the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to return from his religion, and they would give him half of their wealth, and Shayba ibn Rabi'a would marry him to his daughter; and the hypocrites of Madina frightened him that they would kill him if he did not return. So it was revealed. Al-Nahhas said: By His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾, it indicates that he was inclining towards them in order to invite them to Islam, meaning: if Allah, Mighty and Majestic, knew that your inclination towards them would bring benefit, He would not have forbidden you from it, because He is Wise. Then it was said: The address is to him and to his community.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 33, verse 2–3:

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord﴾, meaning the Qur'an. In it there is a prohibition against following the customs of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam), and a command to strive against them and to repudiate them. In it there is also evidence for abandoning the following of opinions (al-ara', personal opinions) in the presence of an explicit text (nass). The address is to him and to his community.

(﴿Indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted﴾) The reading of the majority is with a ta' (you), in address, and this is the preference of Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim. As-Sulami, Abu 'Amr and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "ya'malun" (they do) with a ya', as a report, and likewise in His saying: ﴿Indeed Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾ [al-Fath: 24].[[See vol. 16, p. 380 onward.]]

(﴿And rely upon Allah﴾) That is, depend upon Him in all your circumstances, for it is He who protects you, and whoever forsakes you cannot harm you.

(﴿And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs﴾) meaning Guardian. A certain shaykh from the people of Syria said: A delegation from Thaqif came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked him to grant them enjoyment (of their idol) by al-Lat for a year, which was the idol that Thaqif worshipped, and they said: "So that Quraysh may know our standing with you." The Prophet ﷺ was inclined to this, so the verse was revealed: ﴿And rely upon Allah, and sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs﴾, i.e., He suffices you for what you fear from them. The word "Allah" in ﴿Allah﴾ (as the subject) is in the nominative position because it is the agent. And "wakilan" (as Disposer of affairs) is in the accusative, as a specification (tamyiz) or as a circumstantial qualifier (hal).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 33, verse 4:

There are five issues.

The first: Mujahid said: It was revealed concerning a man from Quraysh who was called Dhu al-Qalbayn (the Possessor of Two Hearts) because of his cunning. He used to say: "I have two hearts in my body, and with each of them I understand better than Muhammad's understanding." He said: "He was from Fihr." Al-Wahidi, al-Qushayri and others said: It was revealed concerning Jamil ibn Ma'mar al-Fihri, who was a man with a retentive memory for what he heard. Quraysh said: "No one retains these things unless he has two hearts." He used to say: "I have two hearts with which I understand better than Muhammad's understanding." When the polytheists were defeated at the Battle of Badr, Jamil ibn Ma'mar was among them. Abu Sufyan saw him in the caravan holding one of his sandals in his hand and the other on his foot. Abu Sufyan said: "What is the condition of the people?" He said: "They have been routed." He said: "Then what is the matter with one of your sandals being in your hand and the other on your foot?" He said: "I was not aware except that they were both on my feet." Thus on that day they understood that if he had had two hearts he would not have forgotten his sandal in his hand.

Al-Suhayli said: Jamil ibn Ma'mar al-Jumahi, who was the son of Ma'mar ibn Habib ibn Wahb ibn Hudhafah ibn Jumah, and the name of Jumah was Taym, was called Dhu al-Qalbayn, and the verse was revealed concerning him. In reference to him the poet says:

"And how can I dwell in Medina after
Jamil ibn Ma'mar has fulfilled his need from it?"

I say: This is how they named him, Jamil ibn Ma'mar. Al-Zamakhshari said: Jamil ibn Asad al-Fihri. Ibn 'Abbas said: The cause of its revelation was that some of the hypocrites said: "Muhammad has two hearts, because he is sometimes in a matter and then turns in another direction for a while, then returns to his original affair." So they said that about him, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, refuted them. It was also said: It was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Khatal. Al-Zuhri and Ibn Hibban said: That was revealed as an illustration concerning Zayd ibn Harithah, when the Prophet ﷺ adopted him. The meaning is: just as a man cannot have two hearts, so a single person cannot be the son of two men. Al-Nahhas said: This view is weak and not valid in the language; it is one of the disconnected reports of al-Zuhri, which Ma'mar related from him. It was also said: It is a proverb coined for the one who makes his wife unlawful to himself by zihar, meaning: just as a man cannot have two hearts, so the wife of one who makes zihar cannot be his mother, unless he has two mothers. It was also said: One of the hypocrites would say: "I have a heart that commands me to do such-and-such, and a heart that commands me to do such-and-such," so the hypocrite is one who has two hearts, and the intended purpose is to refute hypocrisy. It was also said: Belief in Allah, the Exalted, and disbelief cannot be combined in one heart, just as two hearts cannot be combined in one body. The meaning is: two different beliefs cannot be combined in one heart. From the verse as a whole it appears that it negates things the Arabs believed at that time, and it informs of the reality of the matter, and Allah knows best.

The second: The heart is a small piece [[al-Bad'ah (with a fatha, and sometimes with a kasra) is a piece of flesh.]] shaped like a pine cone, which Allah, Exalted, created in the human being and made the place of knowledge, so that the servant comprehends through it what is too vast for books. Allah writes it in it with the divine writing and preserves it in it with the lordly retention, until he comprehends it and forgets nothing of it. It lies between two inclinations: [[al-Lammah (with a fatha) is a thought or a passing impulse that occurs in the heart.]] an inclination from the angel and an inclination from the devil, as the Prophet ﷺ said. It was transmitted by al-Tirmidhi, and it has already been discussed in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 1, p. 187 onward.]]. It is the locus of passing thoughts and whisperings, the place of disbelief and faith, the site of persistence and repentance, and the channel of agitation and tranquility. [[In some copies: (and tranquility and balance).]] The meaning of the verse is that disbelief and faith cannot coexist in the heart, nor guidance and misguidance, nor repentance and persistence. This is a negation of everything anyone might imagine in this regard, whether literally or figuratively, and Allah knows best.

The third: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informs in this verse that no one has two hearts. This also contains a rebuke of the hypocrites mentioned earlier, meaning: there is only one heart, in which there is either faith or disbelief, because the degree of hypocrisy is, as it were, intermediate. Allah negated it and made clear that there is one heart. In this manner a person may cite this verse whenever he forgets something or makes a mistake, saying by way of excuse: "Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his body."

The fourth: The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by zihar your mothers﴾. This refers to a man's saying to his wife: "You are to me like the back of my mother." This is mentioned in the surah "al-Mujadilah" [[See vol. 17, p. 279 onward.]], as will be explained there, if Allah, the Exalted, wills.

The fifth: The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Nor has He made your adopted sons your sons﴾. The scholars of tafsir (exegesis) are unanimous that this was revealed concerning Zayd ibn Harithah. The imams related that Ibn 'Umar said: "We did not call Zayd ibn Harithah anything but Zayd ibn Muhammad, until there was revealed: ﴿Call them by their fathers' names; that is more just in the sight of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 5]." Zayd, as related from Anas ibn Malik and others, had been taken captive from Syria. Horsemen from Tihama captured him, and Hakim ibn Hizam ibn Khuwaylid bought him and gave him to his aunt Khadijah, and Khadijah gave him to the Prophet ﷺ, who freed him and adopted him. He stayed with him for a period. Then his uncle and father came, seeking to ransom him. The Prophet ﷺ said to them, and that was before the Mission: "Let him choose. If he chooses you, he is yours without ransom." He chose slavery with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ over his freedom and his people. At that, Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, said: "O assembly of Quraysh, bear witness that he is my son; he inherits from me and I inherit from him." He used to go around the circles of Quraysh calling them to witness this. His uncle and father were content with this and departed. When he had been captured, his father used to wander around Syria, saying:

"I wept for Zayd and I did not know what had become of him,
whether he is alive and hoped for, or whether death has reached him before his time.
By Allah, I do not know, though I am asking:
has the plain taken you after me, or has the mountain taken you?
Oh, if only I knew! Is there for you, in time, a return?
My sufficiency in this world is your returning to me, a 'bajal.' [[Bajal: like na'am in form and meaning. And abjalahu al-shay': it sufficed him.]]
The sun reminds me of him when it rises,
and his memory comes before me when its setting declines.
If the winds blow, they stir up his memory,
oh, how long has my grief for him been and my anxiety!
I will exert the camel's pace across the earth, striving,
and I will not tire of wandering, though the camels tire.
As long as I live, or until my death comes upon me,
for every man is mortal, even if hope deceives him."

He was then informed that Zayd was in Mecca, so he came to him, and Zayd died while with him. It is also related that he came to him, and the Prophet ﷺ gave him the choice as we have mentioned, and he departed. Mention of his merit, virtue and nobility will come later, at the words of Allah: ﴿So when Zayd had no further need of her, We married her to you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37], if Allah wills. [[See p. 188 of this part.]] Zayd was killed at Mu'tah in the land of Syria in the eighth year after the Hijrah. The Prophet ﷺ had appointed him commander in that expedition and said: "If Zayd is killed, then Ja'far; if Ja'far is killed, then 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah." The three were killed in that expedition, may Allah be pleased with them all. When news of Zayd and Ja'far reached the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he wept and said: "My two brothers, my companions, and my confidants."

This contains six issues.

**First:** His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Call them by [the names of] their fathers﴾. It was revealed concerning Zayd ibn Harithah, as its explanation has already been given. In the words of Ibn Umar: "We did not call Zayd ibn Harithah anything but Zayd ibn Muhammad," which is evidence that *tabanni* (adoption) was practised in the Jahiliyyah and in early Islam, and inheritance and mutual support were established through it, until Allah abrogated (*naskh*, abrogation) that with His saying: ﴿That is more just in the sight of Allah﴾, i.e., more equitable. Thus Allah lifted the ruling of adoption and forbade the use of its term, and by His saying He guided to the fact that it is preferable and more just for a man to be attributed to his father by lineage, so that one says: "So-and-so, son of so-and-so." In the Jahiliyyah, when a man was impressed by another's strength and manners, he would take him into his household and give him the share of a male child in his inheritance, and he would be attributed to him, so it was said: "So-and-so, son of so-and-so."

Al-Nahhas said: This verse abrogates the adoption practice they were upon, and this is an instance of the abrogation of the Sunnah by the Qur'an. He commanded that those whom they had called [by the name of] a father be called by the father known for them. If he had no known father, they were to attribute him to his *wala'* (client-patronage). If he had no known *wala'*, he was to be addressed as "my brother," meaning in religion. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The believers are but brothers﴾. [See vol. 16, p. 322.]

**Second:** If someone attributes a person to his father by way of adoption, then if it is by error, meaning his tongue slips into that without intention, there is no sin upon him and no blame, because of the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And there is no blame upon you for that in which you have erred, but [blame is for] what your hearts have intended﴾. Likewise, if you call a man by other than his father while you believe him to be his father, there is no fault upon you; this was said by Qatadah. This ruling does not apply to a case where a name of adoption has come to prevail over someone, such as the case of al-Miqdad ibn Amr. He had come to be known by the lineage of adoption, so that he was hardly recognised except as al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad, for al-Aswad ibn Abd Yaghuth had adopted him in the Jahiliyyah and he became known by that. When the verse was revealed, al-Miqdad said: "I am the son of Amr," yet the [adoptive] designation remained applied to him. Among those of the past, no one is reported to have been disobedient for using that designation for him, even if he did so deliberately. Likewise Salim, the freedman of Abu Hudhayfah, was called by [the name of] Abu Hudhayfah, and there are others besides these who were adopted, attributed to other than their fathers, became famous for it, and had it prevail over them. This is unlike the case of Zayd ibn Harithah, for it is not permissible to say "Zayd ibn Muhammad" about him. If anyone says it deliberately, he disobeys, because of the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿But [blame is for] what your hearts have intended﴾, i.e., upon you is the blame. And Allah knows best. For this reason He said after it: ﴿And ever is Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾, i.e., Forgiving of the deliberate and Merciful in lifting the sin of error.

**Third:** It has been said that the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted, ﴿And there is no blame upon you for that in which you have erred﴾ is general (*mujmal*), meaning: there is no blame upon you for anything in which you have erred. This was the fatwa of Ata' and many scholars. On this basis, if a man swears that he will not part from his debtor until he collects his right from him, and he takes from him what he considers to be good dinars but then finds them to be counterfeit, there is nothing upon him. Likewise, according to this view, if he swears not to greet so-and-so and greets him while not knowing him, he does not break his oath, because he did not intend that.

The word *ma* (what) is in the genitive position, in response to the *ma* that is with "you have erred." It is also permissible for it to be in the nominative position, by supposing an implied subject, and the meaning would be: "But what you are held accountable for is what your hearts have intended." Qatadah and others said: Whoever attributes a man to other than his father while believing him to be his father, by error, that is among what Allah has lifted blame for. It was also said: It is to say to him in address, "O my son," without intending adoption.

**Fourth:** His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That is your saying by your mouths﴾. The phrase "by your mouths" emphasises the falsity of the statement, meaning that it is a statement with no reality in existence, being merely a verbal utterance. This is like when you say: "I will walk to you on foot," where you only mean by it kindness and honour. Such usage is common, and this meaning has been mentioned before in more than one place. [See vol. 4, p. 267, and vol. 7, pp. 118 onward.]

﴿And Allah says the truth﴾. "The truth" (*al-haqq*) is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, i.e., He says the true saying. And ﴿He guides﴾ means He makes clear, and it is transitive without a preposition.

**Fifth:** *Al-ad'iya'* is the plural of *al-da'i*, who is the one called a son of other than his father, or who claims other than his father. The verbal noun is *al-da'wah* with a kasrah. So Allah commanded calling the adopted ones to their fathers of the loins (*li-l-sulb*). Whoever is not known in this way, and whose lineage is not well known, is to be [regarded as] a *mawla* (client) and a brother in religion.

Al-Tabari mentioned that Abu Bakr recited this verse and said: "I am one whose father is not known, so I am your brother in religion and your *mawla*." The narrator from him said: "By Allah, if he had known that his father was a donkey, he would have claimed him." The transmitters of hadith say about Abu Bakrah: Nufay' ibn al-Harith.

**Sixth:** It is related in the Sahih, from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Abu Bakr, both of whom said: My ears heard it and my heart retained it, Muhammad (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever claims a lineage to other than his father, knowing that he is not his father, Paradise is forbidden to him." And in the hadith of Abu Dharr, that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "There is no man who claims [lineage] for other than his father while knowing it, except that he has disbelieved."

There are nine issues in this matter.

**The first issue:** His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves﴾. Through this verse, God removed rulings that were in force at the beginning of Islam. Among them: the Prophet (ﷺ) would not pray over a dead person who was in debt. When God granted him conquests, he said: "I am closer to the believers than their own selves. Whoever dies leaving a debt, it is my responsibility to pay it; and whoever leaves property, it belongs to his heirs." Reported by the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim). In both of them also: "Whoever of you leaves a debt or dependants, I am his guardian (mawla)." Ibn al-'Arabi said: "The situation has now been reversed by sins. If they leave property, the relatives (asaba) are restricted in it; and if they leave dependants, they are handed over to him. This is the explanation of the guardianship (wilaya) mentioned in this verse, by the explanation and alert of the Prophet (ﷺ)." (And there is no perfume after the bride.) Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Some knowledgeable scholars said: He is closer to them than their own selves, because their selves call them to destruction, while he calls them to salvation." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is supported by his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: 'I am taking hold of your waistbands to save you from the Fire, while you are rushing into it like moths.'" I say: This is a good statement regarding the meaning and interpretation of the verse. The hadith that was mentioned was recorded by Muslim in his Sahih from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "My example and the example of my community is that of a man who kindled a fire, and the insects and moths began to fall into it [[The pronoun referring to this narration is the one who kindled the fire, which is understood from the context.]], while I am taking hold of your waistbands, and you are rushing into it." And from Jabir, similarly, and he said: "And you are slipping out of my hands." The scholars said: The hujza (waistband) is for the trousers, and the ma'qid (knot) is for the wrapper. When a man wants to hold back someone he fears will fall, he grasps that part of him. This is an example of the striving of our Prophet, peace be upon him, for our salvation and his eagerness to free us from the ruins that lie before us. He is therefore closer to us than our own selves. Yet due to our ignorance of the value of this, the dominance of our desires over us, and the triumph of our accursed enemy over our helper, we are more contemptible than the moth and more humiliated than the moth. There is no power and no strength except with God, the Most High, the Mighty! It was also said: "closer to them" means that when he commands something and the self calls to something else, the command of the Prophet (ﷺ) takes precedence. It was also said: "closer to them" means he has more right to judge the believers, so his judgment is implemented upon their selves, that is, in what they judge for themselves that contradicts his judgment.

**The second issue:** Some scholars said: It is obligatory upon the imam (ruler) to pay the debts of the poor from the public treasury (bayt al-mal), following the example of the Prophet (ﷺ), since he explicitly declared this obligation upon himself when he said: "it is my responsibility to pay it." The word al-day'a (dependants), with a fatha on the dad, is the verbal noun of da'a (to be lost). Then it became a name for everything that is about to be lost, such as dependants and children with no one to support them, and property with no one to manage it. Land was called day'a because it is exposed to loss, and its plural is diyaʿ, with a kasra on the dad.

**The third issue:** His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿and his wives are their mothers﴾. God, may He be exalted, honoured the wives of His Prophet (ﷺ) by making them the mothers of the believers, meaning in the obligation of reverence, kindness, honour, and veneration, and in the prohibition of marrying them for men, and in their being veiled, may God be pleased with them, unlike actual mothers. It was said: Since their compassion towards them was like the compassion of mothers, they were given the status of mothers. Then this motherhood does not entail inheritance, like the motherhood of adoption (tabanni). It was permissible to marry their daughters, and they were not made sisters to people. The number of the Prophet's (ﷺ) wives will come, God willing, in the verse of choice [[See p. 164 of this part.]]. People differed over whether they are the mothers of men and women or only the mothers of men, on two views. Al-Sha'bi narrated from Masruq from 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her, that a woman said to her: "O mother!" She said to her: "I am not a mother to you; I am only the mother of your men." Ibn al-'Arabi said: "This is the correct view." I say: There is no benefit in restricting the limitation to permissibility for men only, excluding women. What appears to me is that they are the mothers of men and women, as a way of honouring their right over men and women. This is indicated by the beginning of the verse: "The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves," which necessarily includes men and women. This is also indicated by the hadith of Abu Hurayra and Jabir. Therefore his saying "and his wives are their mothers" refers to all of them. Furthermore, in the codex (mushaf) of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, it reads: "and his wives are their mothers, and he is a father to them." Ibn 'Abbas recited: "from their own selves, and he is a father to them, and his wives are their mothers." [[What is between the brackets is an addition required by the context and is not found in the manuscripts of the original.]] All of this weakens what Masruq narrated, if it is authentic, in terms of preponderance; and if it is not authentic, then the argument from it for restriction falls away, and we remain upon the original principle, which is generality, which comes first to the understanding. [[Thus in the text of J. In K: (the understanding). In Sh: (the understood).]] And God knows best.

**The fourth issue:** His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿And those of kinship are closer to one another in the Book of God than the believers and the emigrants﴾. It was said: He meant by the believers the Ansar (Helpers), and by the emigrants the Quraysh. There are two views on this. The first: It abrogates (naskh) inheritance through emigration. Sa'id narrated from Qatada, who said: In Surat al-Anfal was revealed ﴿And those who believed but did not emigrate, you have no guardianship over them in any way until they emigrate﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 55 onward.]] [al-Anfal: 72]. So the Muslims inherited through emigration, and a Muslim Bedouin would not inherit anything from his Muslim relative who was an emigrant until he emigrated. Then this was abrogated in this surah by his saying: ﴿And those of kinship are closer to one another﴾. The second: That this abrogates inheritance through alliance (hilf) and brotherhood in religion. Hisham ibn 'Urwa narrated from his father, from al-Zubayr: "And those of kinship are closer to one another in the Book of God." That is because we, the company of the Quraysh, when we came to Medina, came with no property. We found the Ansar to be excellent brothers, so we made brotherhood with them, and they bequeathed to us and we bequeathed to them. Abu Bakr made brotherhood with Kharija ibn Zayd, and I made brotherhood with Ka'b ibn Malik. I came and found that the weapons had weighed him down. By God, he died to this world, and no one inherited from him but me, until God, may He be exalted, revealed this verse, and we returned to our rightful heirs. It is established from 'Urwa that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) made brotherhood between al-Zubayr and Ka'b ibn Malik, and Ka'b was carried away wounded (irtatha) on the day of Uhud [[Irtith: that a wounded person is carried from the battlefield while weak, having been overwhelmed by wounds.]], and al-Zubayr came leading him by the reins of his mount. Had Ka'b died that day, leaving behind the sunshine (dhahh) and the wind, al-Zubayr would have inherited from him. [[Al-dhahh (with a kasra): the light of the sun when it has settled upon the ground. He meant: if he had died leaving behind what the sun rises upon and the wind passes over, and by these two he referred to abundance of wealth.]] Then God, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿And those of kinship are closer to one another in the Book of God﴾. Thus God made clear that kinship takes precedence over alliance, so inheritance by alliance was abandoned, and they inherited by kinship. The discussion of the inheritance of relatives by kinship (dhawu al-arham) has already passed in "al-Anfal" [[See vol. 8, p. 59.]]. His saying "in the Book of God" may mean the Qur'an, and it may mean the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), in which He decreed the states of His creation. And "from the believers" is connected to "closer" and not to his saying "those of kinship," by consensus, because that would necessitate restricting it to some of the believers, and there is no disagreement about its generality. This is the resolution of its difficulty, as Ibn al-'Arabi said. Al-Nahhas: ﴿And those of kinship are closer to one another in the Book of God than the believers and the emigrants﴾ — it is permissible that "from the believers" is connected to "those of kinship," so the meaning would be: and those of kinship from among the believers and the emigrants. And it is permissible that the meaning is: closer than the believers. Al-Mahdawi said: It was said that its meaning is: and those of kinship are closer to one another in the Book of God, except what is permitted for the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), that they be called mothers of the believers. And God, may He be exalted, knows best.

**The fifth issue:** There is disagreement over whether they are like mothers regarding mahram status (unmarriageability) and permissibility of looking, on two views. The first: They are mahram; looking at them is not forbidden. The second: Looking at them is forbidden, because the prohibition of marrying them was only to preserve the right of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) concerning them, and part of preserving his right is prohibiting looking at them. Also, 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her, when she wanted a man to enter upon her, would order her sister Asma' to nurse him, so that he would become her nephew through fosterage, and thus become a mahram who may be looked at. As for those whom the Messenger of God (ﷺ) divorced during his lifetime, there is disagreement over whether this prohibition applies to them, on three views. The first: This prohibition applies to them, giving precedence to the sanctity of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The second: It does not apply to them; rather they are like other women, because the Prophet (ﷺ) had affirmed their chastity and said: "My wives in this world are my wives in the Hereafter." The third: Whichever of them the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had consummated the marriage with, her prohibition is established and marrying her is forbidden even if he divorced her, to preserve his sanctity and safeguard his privacy. And whoever he had not consummated the marriage with, this prohibition does not apply to her. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, once intended to stone a woman whom the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had separated from, when she had remarried. She said: "Why this? The Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not place a veil upon me, and I was not named Mother of the Believers." So 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, refrained from her.

**The sixth issue:** Some people said: It is not permissible to call the Prophet (ﷺ) a father, because of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿Muhammad is not the father of any of your men﴾ [al-Ahzab: 40]. But it is said: He is like a father to the believers, as he said: "I am to you in the position of a father; I teach you..." The hadith. Recorded by Abu Dawud. The correct view is that it is permissible to say that he is a father to the believers, meaning in the prohibition of marriage [[Note: in the sense of the prohibition]]. And His saying: ﴿Muhammad is not the father of any of your men﴾ [al-Ahzab: 40] means in lineage. This will come. Ibn 'Abbas recited: "from their own selves, and he is a father to them, and his wives." 'Umar heard this recitation and rejected it and said: "What is its ruling, boy?" He said: "It is in the codex of Ubayy." So he went to him.

He asked him, and Ubayy said to him: "The Qur'an kept me busy, while trading (al-safq, meaning exchange) in the markets kept you busy?" And he spoke harshly to Umar. [[al-Safq: trading.]]

It has been said regarding the words of Lot, peace be upon him, ﴿These are my daughters﴾ [Al-Hijr: 71], that he meant the believing women, i.e., marry them. [[See vol. 9, p. 79 onward.]] This has already been discussed.

The seventh issue: Some scholars said: One may not say that his daughters are sisters of the believers, nor that their maternal uncles are maternal uncles of the believers, or their maternal aunts are the believers' maternal aunts. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: al-Zubayr married Asma' bint Abi Bakr al-Siddiq, and she was the sister of Aisha, but he did not say she was the "aunt of the believers." Others stated this without restriction and said: Mu'awiyah is the "maternal uncle of the believers," meaning in terms of the prohibition (of marriage), not in terms of lineage.

The eighth issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Except that you do a kindness to your allies﴾ means goodness during life and bequest at death, i.e., that this is permissible. This was said by Qatadah, al-Hasan and Ata'. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah said: It was revealed concerning the permissibility of bequeathing to a Jew or a Christian; that is, one does this with a close relative (al-wali) even if he is a disbeliever, for the polytheist is a relative by lineage, not by religion, so a bequest may be made to him. The scholars differed on whether a disbeliever may be appointed as a executor (wasi). Some permitted it and some prohibited it. Some referred the matter to the ruler (al-sultan), among them Malik, may Allah have mercy on him. Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and al-Rummani held that the meaning is: to your allies among the believers. The wording of the verse supports this view, and generalizing the term "wali" is also good. Kinship ties do not exclude the disbeliever, but they do not prevent one from being shown affection, as with a wali of Islam.

The ninth issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That was in the Book, inscribed﴾. "Al-Kitab" may carry the two meanings mentioned earlier regarding "the Book of Allah." "Mastur" comes from your saying "sataртu al-kitab" (I wrote the book) when you make its lines (asṭar) fixed. Qatadah said: That is, written with Allah, mighty and majestic, that a disbeliever should not inherit from a Muslim. Qatadah said: In some recitations it reads "That was written with Allah." Al-Qurazi said: That was in the Torah.

**Allah's words:** "(And [mention] when We took from the Prophets their covenant) [i.e., their pledge] to fulfil what they were entrusted with, and that some of them would give good news of others, and that some would confirm others." That is, it was inscribed when Allah wrote what would come to be, and when Allah the Exalted took the covenants from the Prophets.

"(And from you) O Muhammad, (and from Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, son of Mary)." These five are singled out, although they are included among the Prophets, in order to honour them. It is also said that they are the holders of revealed laws (shara'i') and Books, and the ulu al-'azm (the resolute messengers, the most steadfast of the messengers) and the leaders of their nations. It is possible that this is a stress on severing allegiance between Muslims and disbelievers, meaning: this is something on which the laws did not differ, that is, the laws of the Prophets, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them. At the beginning of Islam there was inheritance on the basis of emigration (hijrah), and emigration is a strongly established obligation in the religion. Then they inherited through kinship together with faith, which is a firm cause. As for inheritance between a believer and a disbeliever, it was not in the religion of any of the Prophets from whom covenants were taken. Therefore, do not compromise in religion and do not side with the disbelievers. A parallel to this is His saying: "He has prescribed for you of the religion that which He enjoined upon Noah," up to His words ﴿and do not become divided therein﴾ [al-Shura: 13].[[See vol. 16, p. 9 onward.]] Among not dividing in religion is abandoning allegiance to the disbelievers. It is also said: the Prophet is more entitled to the believers than they are to themselves; this was inscribed in the Book, and the covenants were taken from the Prophets concerning it.

"(And We took from them a solemn covenant)," that is, a firm and great pledge to fulfil what they undertook of conveying the message, and that some would confirm others. The covenant (mithaq) is an oath by Allah the Exalted, so the second covenant is an emphasis of the first covenant by oath. It is also said: the first is the affirmation of Allah the Exalted, and the second concerns the matter of prophethood. A parallel to this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets: "Whatever I have given you of Book and wisdom, and then there comes to you a messenger confirming what you have, you must believe in him and support him." He said: "Do you affirm and accept My burden on this condition?"﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 81], to the end of the verse. That is, He took from them that they should proclaim that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and that Muhammad (ﷺ) should proclaim that there is no prophet after him. He mentioned Muhammad first in the mention because of what Qatadah reported from al-Hasan, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about the saying of Allah the Exalted, "And when We took from the Prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah," and he said: (I was the first of them in creation and the last of them in resurrection). Mujahid said: this refers to the loins of Adam (peace be upon him).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 33, verse 8:

The Most High said: ﴿That He may question the truthful about their truthfulness﴾. On this there are four opinions. The first: that He may question the prophets about their conveying the message to their peoples; this is related by al-Naqqash. In this there is a warning, meaning: if the prophets are questioned, how much more so others. The second: that He may question the prophets about what their peoples replied to them; this is related by Ali ibn Isa. The third: that He may question the prophets, peace be upon them, about fulfilling the covenant which He took from them; this is related by Ibn Shajara. The fourth: that He may question the truthful tongues about the sincere hearts, and in the Revelation: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers﴾ [al-A'raf: 6]. This has already been discussed [see vol. 7, p. 164]. It has also been said: the benefit of questioning them is the rebuke of the disbelievers, as the Most High said: ﴿Did you say to the people...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116] [see vol. 6, p. 374].

﴿And He has prepared for the disbelievers a painful punishment﴾. This is the punishment of Jahannam (Hell).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 33, verse 9 (part 1 of 4):

It refers to the Battle of the Trench (ghazwat al-Khandaq), the Confederates (al-Ahzab), and Banu Qurayza [[The Battle of the Trench is so named because of the trench that was dug around Medina by the command of the Messenger (ﷺ). As for its being called the Confederates: it is because groups of polytheists gathered to fight the Muslims, namely the Quraysh, Ghatafan, and the Jews.]]. It was a severe condition, followed by blessing, ease, and happiness, and it contained many rulings and remarkable, noble signs. With Allah's help, we will mention from it what suffices, in ten issues.

The first: There is disagreement about what year it took place. Ibn Ishaq said: it was in Shawwal of the fifth year. Ibn Wahb and Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, that the Battle of the Trench was in the fourth year, and that it and the (campaign against) Banu Qurayza occurred on the same day, and that between Banu Qurayza and al-Nadir there were four years. Ibn Wahb said: I heard Malik say: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered fighting from Medina, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿When they came upon you from above you and from below you, and when the eyes shifted and the hearts reached the throats﴾ [al-Ahzab: 10]. He said: That was the day of the Trench. The Quraysh came from this direction, the Jews from this direction, and the Najdis from this direction. Malik means: those who came from above them were Banu Qurayza, and those who came from below them were Quraysh and Ghatafan.

The cause of it was that a group of Jews, among them Kinana ibn al-Rabi' ibn Abi al-Huqayq, Sallam ibn Abi al-Huqayq, Sallam ibn Mishkam, Huyayy ibn Akhtab of al-Nadir, Hawdha ibn Qays, and Abu 'Ammar of Banu Wa'il (all of them Jews), were the ones who formed the confederates, incited, and gathered them. They went out with a group from Banu al-Nadir and a group from Banu Wa'il, came to Mecca, and called them to war against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), promising them help from among themselves for whoever undertook it. The people of Mecca responded to them. Then the aforementioned Jews went out to Ghatafan and called them to the same, and they responded. So Quraysh went out led by Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, and Ghatafan went out, their commander being 'Uyayna ibn Hisn ibn Hudhayfa ibn Badr al-Fazari over Fazara, al-Harith ibn 'Awf al-Murri over Banu Murra, and Mas'ud ibn Rukhayla over Ashja'. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) heard of their gathering and their departure, he consulted his companions, and Salman (al-Farisi) advised digging a trench, and he approved of his opinion. The Muhajirun said that day: "Salman is one of us." And the Ansar said: "Salman is one of us!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Salman is of us, the People of the House." The Trench was the first battle Salman witnessed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he was then a free man. He said: "O Messenger of Allah, when we were in Persia and were besieged, we would dig a trench." The Muslims worked diligently on the trench, while the hypocrites shrank back and began slipping away, concealing themselves, hiding behind one another [[That is, hiding themselves and concealing themselves from one another.]]. Verses of the Qur'an were revealed concerning them, which Ibn Ishaq and others mentioned. Whoever among the Muslims finished his portion returned to help others, until the trench was completed. In it were clear signs and indications of prophethood.

I say: From what we have mentioned of this report, the following points of fiqh (jurisprudence) are derived:

The second: The ruler's consultation with his companions and close associates regarding matters of war. This has already passed in Al 'Imran [[See vol. 4, p. 249 onwards, and vol. 13, p. 194.]] and al-Naml. In it is also fortifying oneself against the enemy by every means possible and using those means, which has passed in more than one place. In it also is that digging the trench is to be divided among the people: whoever finishes his portion helps those who have not finished, for the Muslims are a hand against others. In al-Bukhari and Muslim, on the authority of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, he said: On the day of the Confederates, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dug the trench, I saw him carrying earth from the trench, and the dust covered the skin of his belly, and he had abundant hair. I heard him reciting verses of rajaz from the words of Ibn Rawaha, saying:

"O Allah, had it not been for You, we would not have been guided,
nor would we have given charity, nor would we have prayed.
So send down tranquility upon us,
and make our feet firm if we meet (the enemy)."

As for what was in it of signs, the third: al-Nasa'i related from Abu Sukayna, a man from the freed slaves [[That is, one freed from the Fire.]], from a man of the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered the digging of the trench, a rock appeared to them that stood between them and the digging. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood up, took the pickaxe, placed his garment at the side of the trench, and said: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-An'am: 115], the verse. A third of the rock broke off, and Salman al-Farisi was standing watching. A flash of light came with the blow of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then he struck a second time and said: ﴿And has been fulfilled﴾ [al-An'am: 115], the verse, and another third broke off, and a flash of light appeared, which Salman saw. Then he struck a third time and said: "And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice," the verse, and the remaining third broke off. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out, took his garment, and sat down. Salman said: "O Messenger of Allah, I saw you when you struck! You did not strike a blow except that there was a flash of light with it?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Did you see that, O Salman?" He said: "Yes, by the One who sent you with the truth, O Messenger of Allah!" He said: "When I struck the first blow, the cities of Kisra and what surrounds them, and many cities, were raised up for me, until I saw them with my own eyes." Those of his companions present said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, invoke Allah to open them for us, to give us their families as spoils, and to let us ruin their lands by our hands." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then made supplication. [Then] "I struck the second blow, and the cities of Caesar and what surrounds them were raised up for me, until I saw them with my own eyes." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, invoke Allah, may He exalt, to open them for us, to give us their families as spoils, and to let us ruin their lands by our hands." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made supplication. [Then] "I struck the third blow, and the cities of Abyssinia and the villages surrounding them were raised up for me, until I saw them with my own eyes." At that, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Leave Abyssinia as long as they leave you, and leave the Turks as long as they leave you." [Al-Nasa'i] also related it on the authority of al-Bara', who said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded us to dig the trench, a rock appeared to us on which the pickaxes made no impression. We complained of that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he came, cast off his garment, took the pickaxe, and said: "In the name of Allah," and struck a blow that broke a third of the rock. Then he said: "Allahu Akbar! I have been given the keys of Syria. By Allah, I can now see its red palaces from this place of mine." He said: Then he struck another and said: "In the name of Allah," and broke another third. Then he said: "Allahu Akbar! I have been given the keys of Persia. By Allah, I can now see the white palace of al-Mada'in." Then he struck the third and said: "In the name of Allah," and split the rock, and said: "Allahu Akbar! I have been given the keys of Yemen. By Allah, I can see the gate of San'a'." Abu Muhammad 'Abd al-Haqq authenticated it.

The fourth: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) finished digging the trench, Quraysh came, about ten thousand strong with those who were with them from Kinana and the people of Tihama, and Ghatafan came with those with them from the people of Najd, until they camped beside Uhud. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims went out, until they camped at the back of Sal' [[Sal': a mountain in Medina.]] with three thousand men, pitched their camp, and the trench was between them and the polytheists. He appointed Ibn Umm Maktum over Medina, according to the view of Ibn Shihab. The enemy of Allah, Huyayy ibn Akhtab al-Nadari, went out until he came to Ka'b ibn Asad al-Qurazi, who was the holder of the pact of Banu Qurayza and their chief. He had made a truce with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and had made a covenant with him. When Ka'b ibn Asad heard of Huyayy ibn Akhtab, he closed the door of his fortress against him and refused to open it for him. Huyayy said: "Open for me, my brother." He said: "I will not open for you, for you are an ill-omened man. You call me to break with Muhammad, and I have made a pact with him and covenanted with him, and I have seen from him nothing but fidelity and truthfulness. So I will not break what is between me and him." Huyayy said: "Open for me so that I may speak with you and then depart from you." He said: "I will not do that." He said: "You only fear that I will eat your portion of food with you." Ka'b grew angry and opened for him. Huyayy said: "O Ka'b! I have come to you with the might of an age. I have brought you Quraysh and its lords, and Ghatafan and its leaders. They have pledged together to uproot Muhammad and those with him." Ka'b said to him: "By Allah, you have brought me the humiliation of an age and a cloud with no water in it! Woe to you, O Huyayy! Leave me. I will not do what you call me to." But Huyayy kept on with Ka'b, promising him and deceiving him, until he returned to him and bound himself by covenant to betray Muhammad (ﷺ) and his companions and to march with them. Huyayy ibn Akhtab said to him: "If Quraysh and Ghatafan withdraw, I will enter your protection with those of the Jews who are with me." When the news of Ka'b and Huyayy reached the Prophet (ﷺ), he sent Sa'd ibn 'Ubada, who was the chief of the Khazraj, and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, the chief of the Aws, and he sent with them 'Abd Allah ibn Rawaha and Khawwat ibn Jubayr. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: "Go to Banu Qurayza. If what has been said to us is true, then speak to us in veiled terms and do not dishearten the people. But if it is a lie, then declare it openly to the people." So they went until they came to them, and found them in the worst state that had been reported about them. They insulted the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "There is no covenant between us and him." Sa'd ibn Mu'adh exchanged insults with them, and they exchanged insults with him, and he had a hot temper. Sa'd ibn 'Ubada said to him: "Leave off insulting them, for what lies between us and them is worse than that." Then Sa'd and Sa'd came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) among the body of the Muslims and said: "(They are like) 'Adal and al-Qara" [[They were alluding to the treachery of 'Adal and al-Qara against the companions of al-Raji', Khubayb and his companions.]], alluding to the treachery of 'Adal and al-Qara against the companions of al-Raji', Khubayb and his companions. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) said:

(أَبْشِرُوا يَا مَعْشَرَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ) "Rejoice, O assembly of Muslims!" At that point the trial became severe and the fear intensified. Their enemy came upon the Muslims from above them, that is, from above the valley on the side of the east, and from below them, from the bottom of the valley on the side of the west, until they "assumed about Allah assumptions" (of various kinds). The hypocrites openly displayed much of what they had been concealing. Some of them said: "Our houses are exposed, so let us return to them, for we fear for them." Among those who said this was Aws ibn Qayzi. Others said: "Muhammad promises us the treasures of Kisra and Caesar, yet one of us cannot feel safe for his own self, and he goes out to relieve himself!" Among those who said this was Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, of the Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) remained, and the polytheists remained, for about twenty-some nights, nearly a month, during which there was no fighting between them except for shooting arrows and pebbles. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw that the trial had become severe for the Muslims, he sent to 'Uyayna ibn Hisn al-Fazari and al-Harith ibn 'Awf al-Murri, who were the two leaders of Ghatafan, and offered them a third of the produce of Madinah, so that they would withdraw with those who were with them from Ghatafan, abandon the Quraysh, and return with their people from them. This proposal was a negotiation and not a binding agreement. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw from the two of them that they had relented and were content, he went to Sa'd ibn Mu'adh and Sa'd ibn 'Ubada, informed them of this, and consulted them. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, is this a matter you love, so that we do it for you, or is it something Allah has commanded you, so that we hear and obey, or is it a matter you are doing for us?" He said: "Rather, it is a matter I am doing for you. By Allah, I am doing it only because I have seen the Arabs shoot at you from one bow." Sa'd ibn Mu'adh said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, by Allah, we and these people were upon polytheism and the worship of idols, not worshipping Allah nor knowing Him, and they never hoped to obtain from us a single date except by purchase or as hospitality. Now that Allah has honoured us with Islam, guided us to it, and strengthened us through you, shall we give them our wealth? By Allah, we will give them nothing but the sword until Allah judges between us and them!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was pleased with this and said: "You and that (decision)." He said to 'Uyayna and al-Harith: "Go back, for you have nothing from us but the sword." Sa'd took the document, in which there was no witness, and erased it.

Fifth: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims remained in their condition, while the polytheists besieged them, and there was no fighting between them, except that some horsemen of Quraysh, among them 'Amr ibn 'Abd Wudd al-'Amiri of the Banu 'Amir ibn Lu'ayy, and 'Ikrima ibn Abi Jahl, and Hubayra ibn Abi Wahb, and Dirar ibn al-Khattab al-Fihri, who were the cavalry and the brave men of Quraysh, came until they stood at the trench (khandaq). When they saw it, they said: "This is indeed a stratagem; the Arabs were never acquainted with such a trick." Then they made for a narrow spot in the trench, struck their horses, and the horses leapt across with them, and they crossed the trench and found themselves between the trench and Sal'. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib went out with a group of Muslims until they blocked the breach through which they had crossed. The cavalry advanced towards them. 'Amr ibn 'Abd Wudd had been incapacitated by wounds on the day of Badr, so he did not take part in Uhud, and on the day of the trench he wanted to be seen in his position. When he and his horsemen stood, he called out: "Who will duel?" 'Ali ibn Abi Talib came forward to him and said: "O 'Amr, you have, as has reached us, covenanted with Allah that you will not be called to one of two choices without taking one of them?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then I call you to Allah and Islam." He said: "I have no need of that." He said: "Then I call you to single combat." He said: "O nephew, by Allah, I do not wish to kill you, because of what was between me and your father." 'Ali said to him: "By Allah, I wish to kill you!" 'Amr ibn 'Abd Wudd became enraged, dismounted from his horse, hamstrung it, and went towards 'Ali. They fought on foot and grappled, and the dust rose between them until it hid them. When the dust cleared, 'Ali was seen upon the chest of 'Amr, cutting off his head. When his companions saw that 'Ali had killed him, they burst through the breach with their horses, fleeing in defeat. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said regarding that:

"He supported the stones out of the folly of his opinion, and I supported the religion of Muhammad with my striking."
"I engaged him, and when I left him, he was lying prostrate, like a trunk among soft sand and hillocks."
"I refrained from his garments, though had I been the one who was thrown down, he would have stripped my garments."
"Do not suppose that Allah will abandon His religion and His Prophet, O assembly of the factions."

Ibn Hisham said: Most of the people of knowledge of the biographies doubt that these verses are by 'Ali. Ibn Hisham said: 'Ikrima ibn Abi Jahl threw away his spear that day, as he was fleeing from 'Amr. Hassan ibn Thabit said about that:

"He fled and threw away his spear for us; perhaps, 'Ikrima, you did not do it."
"You turned and ran like the running of a gazelle, which does not stray from the straight path."
"You did not present your back in a reassured manner; as if your back were the back of a young hyena."

Ibn Hisham said: Fur'ul is the young of the hyena. 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, was in the fortress of Banu Haritha, and the mother of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh was with her. Sa'd was wearing a short, tight coat of mail from which his forearm had emerged, and in his hand was his spear, and he was saying:

"Wait a little; a stallion will reach the battle; there is no harm in death when the appointed time has come."

On that day Sa'd ibn Mu'adh was struck by an arrow that severed the al-akhal (a vein in the middle of the forearm). It was disputed who shot him. It was said that Hibban ibn Qays ibn al-'Araqa, of the Banu 'Amir ibn Lu'ayy, shot him; when he struck him he said: "Take it, and I am the son of al-'Araqa." Sa'd said to him: "May Allah blacken your face in the Fire." It was also said that the one who shot him was Khafaja ibn 'Asim ibn Hibban. It was also said that the one who shot him was Abu Usama al-Jushami, an ally of the Banu Makhzum. Regarding that day there is also a curious story involving Hassan and Safiyya bint 'Abd al-Muttalib, mentioned by Ibn Ishaq and others. Safiyya bint 'Abd al-Muttalib, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "On the day of the Confederates we were in the fortress of Hassan ibn Thabit, and Hassan was with us among the women and children, while the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions were in the thick of the enemy and could not withdraw to us. Then a Jew came around, so I said to Hassan: 'Go down to him and kill him.' He said: 'I am not the one for this, O daughter of 'Abd al-Muttalib!' So I took a pole, came down from the fortress, and killed him. I said: 'O Hassan, come down and strip him.' What prevented me from stripping him was only that he was a man. He said: 'I have no need of his spoils, O daughter of 'Abd al-Muttalib!' So I came down and stripped him."

Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: A group of the people of biographies have denied this report about Hassan, and they said: "If Hassan had the cowardice you describe, those whom he used to satirise in the Jahiliyya and in Islam would have mocked him for it, and his son 'Abd al-Rahman would have satirised him for it too, for he often satirised the people among the poets of the Arabs, such as al-Najashi and others."

Sixth: Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud ibn 'Amir al-Ashja'i came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have embraced Islam, but my people do not know of my Islam, so command me as you wish." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "You are only one man from Ghatafan. If you went out and caused dissension among them, if you are able, that would be dearer to us than your remaining with us. So go, for war is deception (khud'a)." Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud went out until he came to Banu Qurayza, with whom he had been a drinking companion in the Jahiliyya, and said: "O Banu Qurayza, you know my affection for you and the special bond between me and you." They said: "Speak, for you are not suspected by us." He said to them: "Quraysh and Ghatafan are not like you. The land is your land; your wealth, your children and your women are in it. Quraysh and Ghatafan have come to fight Muhammad and his companions, and you have backed them against him. If they see an opportunity (nahza) they will seize it; if it is otherwise, they will return to their lands and leave you alone with the man, and you have no strength against him. So do not fight alongside these people until you take hostages from them." Then he went out until he came to Quraysh and said to them: "You know my affection for you, O assembly of Quraysh, and my separation from Muhammad. Word has reached me of a matter that I see as the truth, and I think I should convey it to you as sincere advice, so keep it secret from me." They said: "We will." He said: "You know that the Jews have regretted what they did in abandoning Muhammad, and they have sent to him: 'We have regretted what we did; will it please you if we take from Quraysh and Ghatafan some of their nobles and hand them over to you, so that you may strike their necks, and then we will be with you against those who remain, until we uproot them?'" Then he went to Ghatafan and said the same. When it was the night of Saturday, and that was a favour of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to His Messenger and the believers, Abu Sufyan sent to Banu Qurayza 'Ikrima ibn Abi Jahl with a group from Quraysh and Ghatafan, saying to them: "We are not a people who can remain here; the hoof and the hoofed have perished. So set out at dawn tomorrow for the fighting, so that we may engage Muhammad." They sent back to them: "Today is Saturday, and you know what befell those who transgressed on the Sabbath. Moreover, we will not fight alongside you until you give us hostages." When the messenger returned with this, they (Quraysh and Ghatafan) said: "Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud has spoken the truth, by Allah." Then they turned back...

To them the messengers came, and they said: "By Allah, we will never give you a pledge. So come out with us if you wish; otherwise, there is no covenant between us and you." The Banu Qurayzah said: "Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud has spoken the truth, by Allah." Allah caused discord among them, their word became divided, and Allah sent upon them a violent wind on nights of severe cold. The wind kept overturning their vessels and capsizing their cooking pots.

The Seventh Issue: When the disagreement among them reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he sent Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman to bring him news of them. He went to them and concealed himself among their crowd [[مثلث الغين.]], and he heard Abu Sufyan say: "O assembly of Quraysh, let each man recognize his companion." Hudhayfah said: "So I took hold of the hand of the man beside me and said: 'Who are you?' He said: 'I am so-and-so.'" Then Abu Sufyan said: "Woe to you, O assembly of Quraysh! By Allah, you are not in a place to stay. The horses and the camels have perished [[الكراع: اسم يجمع الخيل. والخف: اسم يجمع الإبل.]], the Banu Qurayzah have broken faith with us, and we have suffered from this wind what you see. No structure stands firm for us, no pot remains steady for us, and no fire can be kindled for us. So depart, for I am departing." Then he leapt onto his camel, and he did not untie its hobbled foreleg except while it was standing.

Hudhayfah said: "Had it not been for the covenant of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with me when he sent me, saying to me: 'Go to the people, learn what they are upon, and do not do anything,' I would have killed him with an arrow." Then I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at the time of their departure, and I found him standing, praying, wrapped in a cloak belonging to one of his wives, embroidered with designs [[قال ابْنُ هِشَامٍ: الْمَرَاجِلُ ضَرْبٌ مِنْ وَشْيِ الْيَمَنِ]]. So I informed him, and he praised Allah.

I say: The report of Hudhayfah is mentioned in Sahih Muslim, and it contains great signs. It was narrated by Jarir from al-A'mash, from Ibrahim al-Taymi, from his father, who said: "We were with Hudhayfah when a man said: 'If I had reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), I would have fought alongside him and displayed great valor.' Hudhayfah said: 'You would have done that? We saw ourselves with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the night of the Confederates, when a violent wind and severe cold seized us.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Is there not a man who will bring us news of the people? Allah will make him with me on the Day of Resurrection?' We remained silent, and none of us answered him. Then he said: 'Is there not a man who will bring us news of the people? Allah will make him with me on the Day of Resurrection?' We remained silent, and none answered him. Then he said: 'Rise, O Hudhayfah, and bring us news of the people.' I had no choice, since he had called me by my name, but to rise. He said: 'Go and bring me news of the people, and do not alarm them against me [[الذعر: الفزع يريد لا تعلمهم بنفسك وامش في خفية لئلا ينفروا منك ويقبلوا علي.]].' When I turned away from him, I felt as though I were walking in a bathhouse [[يقول: كأنما أمشى في حر لم يصبني برد ولا من تلك الريح الشديدة شي ببركة توجيه النبي ﷺ.]] until I reached them. I saw Abu Sufyan warming his back at the fire. I placed an arrow on the belly of the bow and intended to shoot him, but I remembered the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'And do not alarm them against me.' Had I shot him, I would have hit him. So I returned, walking as if in a bathhouse. When I came to him and informed him of the news of the people, and I had finished, I felt warm. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then wrapped me in the extra part of a cloak he used to pray in, and I kept sleeping until morning. When morning came, he said: 'Rise, O sleeper!'"

When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rose in the morning and the Confederates had departed, he returned to Madinah and the Muslims laid down their weapons. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him in the form of Dihyah ibn Khalifah al-Kalbi, upon a mule with a silken saddle-cloth, and said to him: "O Muhammad, if you have laid down your weapons, the angels have not laid down theirs. Indeed, Allah commands you to go out to the Banu Qurayzah, and I am going ahead of you to them, to shake their fortresses."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then commanded a caller, and he called out: "None of you shall pray the Asr except in the land of the Banu Qurayzah." Some people feared that the time would pass, so they prayed before reaching the Banu Qurayzah. Others said: "We will not pray the Asr except where the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded us, even if the time passes." He said: "He did not rebuke either of the two groups. In this is a point of fiqh (jurisprudence), namely the correctness of the mujtahids (jurists exerting independent reasoning). Its explanation has already passed in [the commentary on] al-Anbiya [[راجع ج ١١ ص ٣١١.]]."

Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, when the arrow struck him, prayed to his Lord and said: "O Allah, if You have kept some of the war with Quraysh, then preserve me for it, for there is no people I love more to fight than a people who denied Your Messenger and expelled him. O Allah, and if You have ended the war between us and them, then make it a martyrdom for me, and do not let me die until my eyes are gladdened by the Banu Qurayzah."

Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik, who said: "It reached me that Sa'd ibn Mu'adh passed by Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) and women with her in the fortress (fari') [[في الأصول: (في الأطم الذي فارع). وفارع حصن بالمدينة يقال إنه حصن حسان بن ثابت.]], while he wore a tight-fitting coat of mail, with his sleeves rolled up, and he had a trace of yellow on him, and he was chanting:

"Wait a little, a camel will reach the battle,
There is no harm in death when the appointed time comes."

Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "I fear only that Sa'd will be struck today in his limbs." Then he was struck in his arm vein (akhal).

Ibn Wahb and Ibn al-Qasim narrated from Malik that Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "I have not seen a man more handsome than Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, except the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Then he was struck in his arm vein, and he said: "O Allah, if the war with Qurayzah has ended and nothing remains of it, then take me to You. But if some of it remains, then preserve me until I fight alongside Your Messenger against his enemies." When the judgment regarding the Banu Qurayzah was passed, he died. The people rejoiced and said: "We hope his supplication has been answered."

The Ninth Issue: When the Muslims went out to the Banu Qurayzah, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave the banner to Ali ibn Abi Talib, and he appointed Ibn Umm Maktum over Madinah. Ali and a group with him set out until they reached the Banu Qurayzah and besieged them. They heard the insults against the Messenger (ﷺ), so Ali returned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, do not go to them," and he was disturbed. He said to him: "I think you heard their insult against me. Had they seen me, they would have refrained from that." Then he went to them, and when they saw him they fell silent. He said to them: "You have broken the covenant, O brothers of the apes! May Allah disgrace you and send down His vengeance upon you." They said: "You were not ignorant, O Muhammad, so do not act ignorantly toward us." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then dismounted and besieged them for about twenty-some nights.

Their chief Ka'b offered them three options, so that they might choose whichever they wished: "Either you accept Islam and follow Muhammad in what he brought, and you will be safe. Or you secure your wealth, your women, and your children, for by Allah, you know that he is the one you find written in your Book. Or you kill your sons and your women, then advance and fight until they all die, to the last of them. Or you attack the Muslims on the night of Saturday when they feel secure, and kill them outright." They said to him: "As for Islam, we will not accept it, nor will we oppose the ruling of the Torah. As for killing our sons and women, what good would the poor among us be after that? We will not transgress on the Sabbath." Then they sent for Abu Lubabah, who was an ally of the Banu Amr ibn Awf and of the rest of the Aws. He came to them, and they gathered around him their sons, women, and men, and said to him: "O Abu Lubabah, do you think we should submit to the judgment of Muhammad?" He said: "Yes," and he pointed with his hand to his throat, meaning: "It is slaughter if you do." Then Abu Lubabah immediately regretted it, and he knew that he had betrayed Allah and His Messenger, and that it was a matter Allah would not conceal from His Prophet (ﷺ).

He went to Madinah and did not return to the Prophet (ﷺ). He tied himself to a pillar and swore that he would not leave his place until Allah accepted his repentance. His wife used to untie him at the time of each prayer. Ibn Uyaynah and others said: "Concerning him was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not betray Allah and the Messenger, nor betray your trusts﴾ [[راجع ج ٧ ص ٣٩٤.]] [al-Anfal: 27], the verse." He also swore that he would never enter the land of the Banu Qurayzah, at any place where he had committed the sin. When the news of what Abu Lubabah had done reached the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "As for him, had he come to me, I would have asked forgiveness for him. But since he has done what he did, I will not release him until Allah releases him." Then Allah the Exalted revealed concerning the matter of Abu Lubabah: ﴿And others who have acknowledged their sins﴾ [[راجع ج ٨ ص ٢٤٢.]] [al-Tawbah: 102], the verse. When the Qur'an came down concerning him, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded that he be released.

When morning came, the Banu Qurayzah surrendered to the judgment of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The Aws rushed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, you know that they are our allies. You have already granted Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul his request concerning the Banu Nadir, who were allies of the Khazraj. So let not our share be lower and less with you than the share of others, for they are our clients." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: "O assembly of the Aws, are you not content that a man from among you should judge concerning them?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Then the matter is in the hands of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had pitched a tent for him in the mosque, so that he could visit him nearby during his illness from the wound he had received at the Trench. He judged concerning them that the fighting men should be killed, the children and women taken captive, and their property divided. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "You have judged concerning them by the judgment of Allah the Exalted, from above seven heavens [[أرقعة جمع رقيع والرقيع السماء سميت بذلك لأنها رقعت بالنجوم.]]."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded that they be taken out to a place in the market of Madinah, today's market at the time of Ibn Ishaq, and he had trenches dug there. Then he commanded (peace be upon him), and their necks were struck in those trenches. On that day Huyayy ibn Akhtab and Ka'b ibn Asad were killed, and they were the leaders of the people. They numbered between six hundred and seven hundred. Huyayy was wearing a rose-colored garment [[أي بلون الورد حين أن ينفتح.]], which had been cut from every side into pieces the size of a fingertip, one piece at a time, so that it would not be stripped from him. When he looked at the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he was brought before him, with his hands bound to his neck with a rope, he said: "By Allah, I did not blame myself for my enmity toward you. But whoever Allah forsakes will be forsaken."

Then he said: "O people, there is no harm in the command of Allah—a Book, a decree, and a great slaughter (al-malhama: a great battle with much killing) that was written upon the Children of Israel." Then he sat down, and his neck was struck. And among their women, one woman was killed: she was Bunana, the wife of al-Hakam al-Qurazi, who dropped a millstone upon Khallad ibn Suwayd and killed him.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered that every one of them who had grown pubic hair be killed, and that whoever had not grown it be spared. 'Atiyya al-Qurazi was among those who had not grown it, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spared him, and he is mentioned among the Companions.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave the children of al-Zubayr ibn Bata to Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, and he spared them. Among them was 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Zubayr, who embraced Islam and had companionship (with the Prophet).

The Prophet (ﷺ) also gave Rifa'a ibn Samaw'al al-Qurazi to Umm al-Mundhir Salma bint Qays, the sister of Sulayt ibn Qays of the Banu al-Najjar, and she had prayed towards both qiblas. Rifa'a embraced Islam and had companionship and narration (of hadith).

Ibn Wahb and Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik, who said: Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas came to Ibn Bata—and Ibn Bata had a favour owed to him—and said: "I have asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to grant you to me, in return for the favour you did me." He said: "That is what a generous man does for a generous man." Then he said: "But how can a man live who has no child and no family?" So Thabit came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and told him of that, and he gave him his family and children. He came and informed him, and he said: "How can a man live who has no property?" So Thabit came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked for him, and he gave him his property. He returned to him and informed him. He said: "What has become of Ibn Abi al-Huqayq, the one whose face was like a Chinese mirror?" He said: "He has been killed." He said: "And what has become of the two assemblies, meaning the Banu Ka'b ibn Qurayza and the Banu 'Amr ibn Qurayza?" He said: "They have been killed." He said: "And what has become of the two groups?" He said: "They too have been killed." He said: "Then your covenant is void, and I will never draw a bucket from it again"—meaning the palm trees.
