"So join me with them." He refused to kill him, and another man killed him. The favour that Ibn Bata had owed to Thabit was that Thabit had captured him on the day of Bu'ath, shaved his forelock, and released him.

The tenth issue: The Prophet (ﷺ) divided the wealth of the Banu Qurayza, giving the mounted warrior three shares and the foot soldier one share. It has also been said: the mounted warrior receives two shares and the foot soldier one share. On that day the Muslims had thirty-six horses. From their captives there fell to the Prophet (ﷺ) Rayhana bint 'Amr ibn Janafa (also said with a khaʼ, "Khanafa"), of the Banu 'Amr ibn Qurayza, and she remained with him until he died (ﷺ). It is also said that the booty of Qurayza was the first booty in which a share was given to both the mounted and the foot soldier, and the first booty in which the one-fifth (khums) was levied. It has already been mentioned that the first of that was in the expedition of 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh, and Allah knows best.

Abu 'Umar said: The reconciliation of this is that the booty of Qurayza was the first booty in which the one-fifth was applied after the revelation of His words: ﴿And know that whatever you gain of booty, a fifth of it is for Allah and for the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 41], and so on. 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh had already applied the one-fifth in his expedition before that, then the Qur'an was revealed in accordance with what he had done, and this was among his virtues, may Allah have mercy on him.

The conquest of Qurayza took place at the end of Dhu al-Qa'da and the beginning of Dhu al-Hijja of the fifth year after the Hijra. When the affair of the Banu Qurayza was complete, the supplication of the excellent, righteous man Sa'd ibn Mu'adh was answered: his wound burst open and his vein was opened, his blood flowed, and he died, may Allah be pleased with him. He is the one of whom the hadith says: "The Throne of the Merciful shook at his death," meaning the inhabitants of the Throne among the angels rejoiced at the arrival of his soul and were stirred for him. Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik, who said: Yahya ibn Sa'id told me: "Seventy thousand angels descended at the death of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, who had never descended to earth before." Malik said: "On the day of the Trench, only four or five of the Muslims were martyred." I (al-Qurtubi) say: Those martyred on the day of the Trench from among the Muslims were six persons, as mentioned by the scholars of biography: Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, Abu 'Amr, of the Banu 'Abd al-Ashhal; Anas ibn Aws ibn 'Atik; 'Abd Allah ibn Sahl, and both of these are also of the Banu 'Abd al-Ashhal; al-Tufayl ibn al-Nu'man; and Tha'laba ibn Ghanama (in al-Mawahib al-Ladunniyya and al-Isaba: "Tha'laba ibn 'Unma," with a closed 'ayn and nun), both of whom are of the Banu Salama; and Ka'b ibn Zayd of the Banu Dinar ibn al-Najjar, struck by a stray arrow (sahm gharb) and killed, may Allah be pleased with them.

Three of the disbelievers were killed: Munabbih ibn 'Uthman ibn 'Ubayd ibn al-Sabbaq ibn 'Abd al-Dar, struck by an arrow from which he died in Mecca. It has also been said that it was 'Uthman ibn Umayya ibn Munabbih ibn 'Ubayd ibn al-Sabbaq. And Nawfal ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi, who plunged into the trench, fell into it, and was killed; the Muslims overcame his body. It is related from al-Zuhri that they offered the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ten thousand dirhams for his body, and he said: "We have no need for his body or its price," so he left them free to take it. And 'Amr ibn 'Abd Wudd, whom 'Ali killed in single combat, has already been mentioned.

From the Muslims, Khallad ibn Suwayd ibn Tha'laba ibn 'Amr of the Banu al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj was martyred on the day of Qurayza, when a woman of the Banu Qurayza dropped a millstone upon him and killed him. Abu Sinan ibn Mihsan ibn Hurthan al-Asadi, brother of 'Ukkasha ibn Mihsan, died during the siege, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) buried him in the cemetery of the Banu Qurayza, which Muslims who live there today use as their burial ground. No one else was struck, and the Quraysh disbelievers did not attack the believers after the Trench.

Al-Darimi, Abu Muhammad, related in his Musnad: Yazid ibn Harun informed us, from Ibn Abi Dhi'b, from al-Maqburi, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Sa'id al-Khudri, from his father, who said: "We were detained on the day of the Trench until a great part of the night had passed (hawiyy: a long time), until we were relieved, and that is the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿And Allah sufficed the believers in fighting, and Allah is ever Strong and Mighty﴾ [al-Ahzab: 25]. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded Bilal, and he gave the iqama and prayed the noon prayer, performing it well as he used to at its time; then he commanded him, and he gave the iqama for the afternoon prayer and prayed it; then he commanded him, and he gave the iqama for the sunset prayer and prayed it; then he commanded him, and he gave the iqama for the night prayer and prayed it. This was before the revelation of: ﴿If you fear, then on foot or riding﴾ [al-Baqara: 239]." Al-Nasa'i also recorded it. This issue has already passed in Surah Ta-Ha. We have mentioned in this battle many rulings for whoever reflects on them, in ten issues. Now we return to the beginning of the verses, and they are nineteen verses that comprise what we have mentioned.

His Exalted saying: ﴿When there came upon you armies﴾, meaning the confederates (al-ahzab).

(Then We sent upon them a wind): Mujahid said: it is the east wind (al-saba), sent upon the confederates on the day of the Trench, until it overturned their cooking pots and tore up their tents. He said: "And the armies are the angels, who did not fight that day." 'Ikrima said: "The south wind said to the north wind on the night of the Confederates: 'Go forth to support the Prophet (ﷺ).' The north wind said: 'Mahwa (the north wind, named for erasing the clouds and carrying them away, a definite noun that takes no tanwin and no article) does not travel by night.' So the wind that was sent against them was the east wind (al-saba)." Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I was aided by the east wind, and 'Ad were destroyed by the west wind (al-dabur)." This wind was a miracle of the Prophet (ﷺ), because the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims were near it, with nothing between them and it except the width of the Trench, yet they were safe from it and had no knowledge of it.

(And armies you did not see): it is also read with the ya' (yara), meaning the polytheists did not see them. The commentators said: Allah sent the angels against them, and they uprooted the tent pegs, cut the ropes of the tents, extinguished the fires, overturned the cooking pots, the horses ran about among one another, Allah cast terror into them, and the angels' takbir increased in the sides of the camp, until the chief of every tent would call: "O Banu so-and-so, come to me!" When they gathered, he would say to them: "Escape! Escape!" because of the terror Allah had cast upon them.

(And Allah is ever Seeing of what you do): it is also read with the ya' (ya'malun), as a report, and this is the reading of Abu 'Amr. The rest read it with the ta' (ta'malun), meaning of digging the trench and guarding against the enemy.

When they came at you from above you and from below you, and when the eyes swerved and the hearts reached the throats, and you were thinking about Allah in various ways (ﷺ)...

Wait, I should translate faithfully and completely. Here is the translation:

"Idh" (when) is in the accusative position, with the sense of "remember." The same applies to "And when a group of them said" (Qur'an 33:13). "From above you" means from above the valley, its upper part from the direction of the east. From it came Awf ibn Malik with the Banu Nasr, Uyayna ibn Hisn with the people of Najd, and Tulayha ibn Khuwaylid al-Asadi with the Banu Asad. "And from below you" means from the bottom of the valley from the direction of the west. From it came Abu Sufyan ibn Harb with the people of Makkah, Yazid ibn Jahsh with the Quraysh, and Abu al-A'war al-Sulami came, accompanied by Huyayy ibn Akhtab the Jew, with the Jews of Banu Qurayza, together with Amir ibn al-Tufayl, from the direction of the trench.

"And when the eyes swerved" means they stared fixedly. It was also said: they inclined, so they did not turn except to their enemy, in astonishment from the extreme of the terror.

"And the hearts reached the throats" means they moved from their places in the chests until they reached the throats, which are the gullets (al-halaqim); its singular is hanjara. Had the throats not been too narrow for them, they would have come out. This is the statement of Qatada. It was also said: it is an intensification in the manner of the Arabs, by way of the implied "kad" (nearly). The poet said:

"When we become angry with a Mudari anger, we tear the veil of the sun, or it drips blood"

meaning: it nearly dripped. It is said that the lung opens up in fear, so the heart rises until it nearly reaches the throat, as an image; for this reason the coward is described as "his lungs have swelled." It was also said that this is a proverbial image of the intensity of fear, with the hearts reaching the throats even though they did not leave their places while life remained. Ikrima said this meaning. Hammad ibn Zayd narrated from Ayyub from Ikrima that he said: their terror reached its peak. The more apparent meaning is that he meant the agitation of the heart and its pounding, as if, from the intensity of its agitation, it reached the throat. The hanjara and the hunjur (with an added nun) are the windpipe.

"And you were thinking about Allah in various ways" – al-Hasan said: the hypocrites thought that the Muslims would be uprooted, and the believers thought that they would be given victory. It was also said: this is an address to the hypocrites, meaning you said, "Muhammad and his companions have perished."

The readers differed concerning the words "al-zununa" (al-ẓunūnā), "al-rasula" (al-rasūlā) and "al-sabila" (al-sabīlā) at the end of the surah. Nafi' and Ibn Amir kept their alif both in pause and in continuation. It is narrated from Abu Amr and al-Kisai, holding to the writing of the Mushaf, the Mushaf of Uthman and all the Mushafs in all the lands, and this was chosen by Abu Ubayd, except that he said: the reader should not run these words into what follows but should pause on them. They said: this is because the Arabs do so in the rhyme of their poems and its hemistich endings. He said:

"We brought the mares' colts, the caravans... / the rear ranks summon the front ranks"

Abu Amr, al-Jahdari, Ya'qub and Hamza read with their omission both in continuation and in pause. They said: it is an added alif in the writing, just as the alif was added in His saying, "and they would have hastened through your midst" (9:47), and they wrote it so, and other than this. As for poetry, it is a matter of necessity, unlike the Qur'an, which is the most eloquent of languages and has no necessity in it. Ibn al-Anbari said: no one who read "al-zunun, al-sabil, al-rasul" without alif in the three words opposed the Mushaf, and they were written in the Mushaf with an alif, because the alif in "atana" and the one entering at the beginning of "al-rasul, al-zunun, al-sabil" suffices from the final, late alif, just as the alif of Abjad suffices from the alif of hawwaz. In this there is another proof: that the alif was given the status of the fatha and what is attached as a support to the preceding vowel, and the intention in it is dropping; when it is treated this way, the alif together with the fatha is like one thing, and pause requires their dropping, and it is treated as though the form of the alif in writing does not require a place in pronunciation, and it is dropped from the writing as in "sihran" and in "fatara al-samawati wal-ard" and in "wa'adna Musa" and what resembles them of what is dropped from writing while it exists in pronunciation. There is a third proof: that it was written according to the dialect of those who say "laqitu al-rajula." It was also read according to the dialect of those who say "laqitu al-rajul," without alif. Ahmad ibn Yahya reported to us from a group of the people of language that they transmitted from the Arabs "qama al-rajulu" with a waw, and "marartu bi al-rajili" with a ya', in continuation and pause, and "laqitu al-rajula" with an alif in both states. The poet said:

"Asa'ilatun Umayra 'an abiha... khilal al-jaysh ta'taruf al-rikaba"

He kept the alif in "al-rikaba" according to this dialect. Another said:

"Idha al-jawza'u ardafat al-thurayya... zanantu bi-al-i Fatima al-zununa"

Upon this dialect Nafi' and others built. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin and al-Kisai read with its affirmation in pause and its omission in continuation. Ibn al-Anbari said: whoever joins without alif and pauses with alif may justifiably argue that the alif was needed at the pause out of eagerness to preserve the fatha, and that the alif supports it and strengthens it.

"Hunā" is for what is near in place, "hunālika" for what is far, and "hunāka" for what is in the middle. It can also be used to point to a time, meaning: at that time the believers were tested, so that the sincere might be distinguished from the hypocrite. This testing consisted of fear, fighting, hunger, siege and close combat.

(﴿وَزُلْزِلُوا زِلْزَالًا شَدِيدًا﴾) meaning they were shaken with a severe shaking.

Al-Zajjaj said: every verbal noun (maṣdar) of the doubled (muḍā῾af) form on the pattern fi῾lāl may be read with a kasra or a fatḥa, as in qalqaltuhu qilqālan and qalqālan, and zulzilū zilzālan and zalzālan. The kasra is the better reading, because the non-doubled forms take the kasra, as in daḥraljtuhu diḥrājan. The reading of the common people is with a kasra on the zāy. ῾Āṣim and al-Jaḥdarī read zalzālan with a fatḥa on the zāy.

Ibn Salām said: meaning they were moved by fear with a violent movement. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it is their being displaced from their places until there remained for them only the place of the trench. It was also said: it is their agitation away from what they had been upon, so some of them were agitated in themselves and some were agitated in their religion.

"Hunālika" may have as its governing word "ubtuliya" (was tested), in which case one does not pause on "hunālika." It may also be that its governing word is "wa-taẓunnūna billāhi al-ẓunūnā," in which case one pauses on "hunālika."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 33, verse 12:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease say﴾, i.e., doubt and hypocrisy.

(﴿What Allah and His Messenger promised us was nothing but delusion﴾), i.e., falsehood of speech. The reason was that Tu'mah ibn Ubayriq, Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, and a group of about seventy men said on the day of the Trench: "How does he promise us the treasures of Chosroes and Caesar, while none of us can relieve himself?" They only said this after what the Prophet (ﷺ) had said while striking the rock spread among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), as previously mentioned in the hadith of al-Nasa'i. So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 33, verse 13:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when a group of them said, "O people of Yathrib, there is no place for you, so return.">﴾ The word ṭāʾifah (group) applies to one person and more. Here it refers to Aws ibn Qayzi, father of ʿArabah ibn Aws, about whom al-Shammakh says:

"When a banner is raised for glory, ʿArabah receives it with the right hand."

Yathrib is al-Madinah, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) named it Ṭaybah and Ṭābah. Abu ʿUbaydah said: Yathrib is the name of a land, and al-Madinah is a district within it. Al-Suhayli said: It was called Yathrib because the one who settled it from the ʿAmaliq was named Yathrib ibn ʿUmayl ibn Mahlaʾil ibn ʿAwaḍ ibn ʿAmlaq ibn Lawdh ibn Iram. There is disagreement regarding some of these names. [[In the Mu'jam al-Buldan of Yaqut: (Yathrib ibn Qani'ah ibn Mahlaʾil ibn Iram, ʿUbayl ibn ʿAwaḍ ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh, peace be upon him).]] The Banu ʿUmayl [[In Mu'jam al-Buldan: (al-Kalbi said: The ʿAmaliq expelled the Banu ʿUqayl, who were brothers of ʿAd, and they settled in al-Juhfah ...).]] are those who inhabited al-Juhfah, and the torrents swept them away there, and from this al-Juhfah got its name.

"Lā muqāma lakum" with a fatḥah on the mim is the reading of the common readers. Ḥafṣ, al-Sulami, al-Jahdari and Abu Haywah read it with a ḍammah on the mim, making it a verbal noun from aqāma yuqīmu, meaning "there is no staying," or a place where they stay. Whoever reads it with a fatḥah takes it as a noun of place, meaning "there is no place for you in which to stay." ﴿So return﴾ means to your dwellings. They ordered them to flee from the army of the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn ʿAbbas said: The Jews said to ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul and his companions among the hypocrites: "What compels you to kill yourselves at the hand of Abu Sufyan and his companions? Return to al-Madinah, for we are with the people, and you will be safe."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And a party of them asked permission of the Prophet﴾ to return to their homes in al-Madinah, and they were the Banu Harithah ibn al-Harith, according to the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas. Yazid ibn Ruman said: It was Aws ibn Qayzi who said this on behalf of a group of his people.

(﴿They say, "Indeed our houses are exposed (ʿawrah)"﴾), that is, unprotected and vulnerable, not secure, and they are on the side facing the enemy. It was also said: open to thieves because they are empty of men. It is said: a house that is muʿwirah and dhāt ʿawrah when entry into it is easy. It is said: the place became ʿawir, ʿawar, so it is ʿawir, and the houses are ʿawirah. And aʿwar, so he is muʿwir. It was also said: ʿawirah is dhāt ʿawrah. Every place that is neither protected nor concealed is ʿawrah, as al-Harawi said. Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrimah, Mujahid and Abu Rajaʾ al-ʿUtaridi read ʿawirah with a kasrah on the waw, meaning with short walls and gaps in them. The Arabs say: the house of so-and-so is ʿawirah when it is not secure. And a horseman has become aʿwar when a gap has appeared in him for striking and thrusting. The poet says:

"Whenever you meet them, you will not find in the house one who is exposed,
nor a guest stricken, nor a neighbor left destitute."

Al-Jawhari said: ʿawrah is every gap feared in a frontier or in war. Al-Nahhas said: It is said aʿwar al-makan when a ʿawrah becomes apparent in it, and aʿwar al-fariss when the place of weakness in him becomes evident. Al-Mahdawi said: Whoever pronounces the waw with a kasrah in ʿawrah is an anomalous reading, and similar to it is their saying: rajul ʿawr, meaning he has nothing. [[The sources are confused here: in Sh: (wa-rajul aʿwar, i.e., he has nothing). In J: (rajul ʿawr kawr ...) with a kaf. In K: (wa-rajul ʿawr lawr ...) with a lam. Perhaps the last word is an echo, but we did not find it in its usual sources.]] Analogically it should have been treated as a defective noun, so it would be said ʿārin, like yawm rāḥ [[i.e., having wind and having wealth.]] and rajul māl; the original forms of both are rawḥ and mawl. Then He, may He be exalted, said: (﴿But they are not exposed (ʿawrah)﴾), denying their claim and rejecting what they had mentioned.

(﴿They intend only to flee﴾), that is, they intend only to run away. It was said: from killing. It was also said: from the religion. Al-Naqqash related that this verse was revealed concerning two clans of the Ansar, the Banu Harithah and the Banu Salamah, who intended to abandon their posts on the day of the Trench, and concerning them Allah, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿When two groups among you were about to lose heart﴾ [Al ʿImran: 122], and so on. When this verse was revealed they said: "By Allah, what we had intended did not grieve us, since Allah is our Protector." Al-Suddi said: Those who sought permission from him were two men of the Ansar from the Banu Harithah, one of them Abu ʿArabah ibn Aws, and the other Aws ibn Qayzi. Al-Dahhak said: Eighty men returned without his permission.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 33, verse 14:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if it had been entered upon them from its surroundings﴾, and these are the houses or the city, meaning from its sides and its flanks. The singular is qutr (side, flank), which is the side and the region. Likewise al-qutr is a dialectal variant of al-qutr [in the sense of the same root meaning], i.e., al-qutr (the side).

(Then they were asked for fitnah, they would have given it) meaning they would have come to it. This is according to the reading of Nafi' and Ibn Kathir with the short vowel (alif-less form, ataw). The rest read it with the long vowel (aatawha), meaning they would have given it from themselves, and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim. It has come in a hadith: the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) were tortured for the sake of Allah and were asked for shirk, and every one of them gave what they were asked except Bilal. And in this is evidence for the reading with the long vowel, from giving (i'ta'). And the saying of Him, exalted is He, "And they had already covenanted with Allah before, that they would not turn their backs" (Qur'an 33:15), indicates the reading with the short vowel, "la-atawha" (they would have come to it). As for "fitnah" here, there are two views: the first is that they were asked for fighting in partisanship, they would have hastened to it; this was said by al-Dahhak. The second: "Then they were asked for shirk, they would have answered it hastening"; this was said by al-Hasan.

(But they would not have delayed in it except briefly) meaning in the city after giving the disbelief, except briefly, until they would be destroyed; this was said by al-Suddi, al-Qutaybi, al-Hasan and al-Farra'. Most of the exegetes said: meaning they would not have held back from the fitnah of shirk except briefly, and they would have answered with shirk hastening, and that is due to the weakness of their intentions and the excess of their hypocrisy. So if the confederates had mixed with them, they would have displayed disbelief.

Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 33, verse 15:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they had certainly made a covenant with Allah before﴾, meaning before the Battle of the Trench (Ghazwat al-Khandaq) and after Badr. Qatadah said: This was because they had been absent from Badr, and they saw what Allah had granted the people of Badr of honour and victory, so they said: "If Allah makes us witness a battle, we will certainly fight." Yazid ibn Ruman said: They were the Banu Harithah. On the day of Uhud they intended to lose heart along with the Banu Salamah. When what was revealed about them was revealed, they made a covenant with Allah that they would not return to the like of that. So Allah mentioned to them what they had given of themselves. ﴿And the covenant of Allah is ever to be questioned﴾, meaning it will be asked about (mas'ul 'anhu). Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: They were seventy men who pledged allegiance to the Prophet (ﷺ) on the night of al-Aqabah, and they said: "Stipulate for yourself and for your Lord whatever you wish." He said: "I stipulate for my Lord that you worship Him and do not associate anything with Him, and I stipulate for myself that you protect me from what you protect your women, your wealth and your children from." They said: "What then will be ours if we do that, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "For you is victory in this world and Paradise in the Hereafter." This is the meaning of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the covenant of Allah is ever to be questioned﴾, meaning that Allah will indeed question them about it on the Day of Resurrection.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say: Flight will never benefit you if you flee from death or killing﴾. That is, whoever's appointed term has come will die or be killed, so fleeing does not benefit.

(And then you will not be given enjoyment except for a little) That is, in this world after fleeing, until your appointed terms run out, and everything that is coming is near. Al-Sajiyy transmitted from Ya'qub al-Hadrami: "wa-idhan la yumatta'un" with a ya' (يُمَتَّعُونَ). In some transmissions it is "wa-idhan la tumatta'u" with a nasb by "idhan" (إذاً), and the raf' (تُمَتَّعُونَ) is in the sense of "wa-la tumatta'un." "Idhan" (إذاً) is mulghah (cancelled, i.e. not functioning as a governing particle), though its i'mal (operating, i.e. governing the verb in the subjunctive) is permissible. This is its ruling when it is preceded by the waw or the fa'. But when it begins a sentence, it governs the verb in the accusative, so you say: "Idhan ukrimak" (إذا أكرمك).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 33, verse 17:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: "Who is it that can protect you from Allah?"﴾ That is, who can prevent you from Him?

(﴿If He intends for you harm⦆) That is, destruction.

(﴿Or intends for you mercy⦆) That is, good, victory, and well-being.

(﴿And they will not find for themselves besides Allah any protector or any helper⦆) That is, no close relative who benefits them, nor any supporter who helps them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 33, verse 18:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah already knows those of you who hinder﴾, i.e., those among you who obstruct [people] from the Prophet ﷺ. It is derived from "‘āqanī ‘an kadhā," meaning he diverted me from it. And ʿawwaqa, with intensification (wa-l-qāʾilīna li-ikhwānihim halumma ilaynā, "and those who say to their brothers, 'Come here to us'"), is in the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz. Others say halummū for a group and halummī for a woman, because the original is that "hā," which serves as an alert, was joined to "lamma," then the alif was dropped for lightness and it was built on fatḥah (the vowel "a"). Neither kasrah nor ḍammah is permitted in it, because it is indeclinable. The meaning of halumma is "come forward." "These are two groups," meaning: among you are those who discourage and hinder. Al-ʿawq is prevention and diversion; it is said ʿāqahu yaʿūquhu ʿawqan, and ʿawwaqahu and iʿtāqahu have the same meaning. Muqatil said: they are ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions, the hypocrites.

"And those who say to their brothers, 'Come here to us.'" Regarding them there are three opinions. The first: they are the hypocrites, who said to the Muslims: "Muhammad and his companions are only a mouthful [[i.e., a small number that one head can satisfy; it is the plural of ākil, eater.]], and he and those with him are doomed, so come to us." The second: they are the Jews of the Banu Qurayza, who said to their brothers among the hypocrites: "Come here to us," meaning come to us and separate from Muhammad, for he is doomed, and if Abu Sufyan prevails he will not leave any of you alive. The third: what Ibn Zayd related, that a man from among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ was among the spears and swords, and his brother, who was from his mother and father, said: "Come here to me, you have been surrounded along with your companion," meaning you and your companion have been encircled. He said to him: "You lie. By Allah, I will inform him of your matter," and he went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to inform him, but he found that Jibril, upon him be peace, had descended to him with the words of the Exalted: "Allah already knows those of you who hinder and those who say to their brothers, 'Come here to us.'" This was mentioned by al-Mawardi and al-Tha'labi as well. Its wording: Ibn Zayd said: this was on the day of the Confederates. A man went out from the presence of the Prophet ﷺ and found his brother before him a loaf, roast meat, and date wine. He said to him: "You are in this while we are among the spears and swords?" He said: "Come here to this, for it has been prepared for you and your companions, and by the One you swear by, Muhammad will never be able to bear it." He said: "You lie." So he went to the Prophet ﷺ to inform him, and found that Jibril had descended upon him with this verse.

(And they do not come to the fighting except a little) out of fear of death. It was also said: they do not attend the battle except for show and to be seen.

This is the commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on Surah 33, verse 19:

The statement of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Stingy towards you﴾, meaning, miserly towards you, that is, with regard to digging the trench and spending in the way of Allah. This is said by Mujahid and Qatadah. It is also said: stingy with fighting alongside you. And it is said: stingy with spending on your poor and needy.

It is also said: stingy with the spoils when they obtain them. This is said by al-Suddi. The word is in the accusative as a *hal* (circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the subject at the time of the action). Al-Zajjaj said: Its accusative case, according to al-Farra', has four possible analyses. The first: it is in the accusative for *dhamm* (dispraise). It may also be, in his view, an accusative with the meaning of "they obstruct, being stingy." It may also be that the implied construction is: "and those who say, being stingy." And it may be, in his view, [ "And they do not come to the battle except a little," being stingy, meaning that they come to it stingy towards the poor with the spoils [[What is between the brackets is from al-Nahhas's book, and it is clear. The wording of the original sources is: "And they do not come to the battle except a little, coming to it stingy, that is, stingy towards the poor with the spoils, cowardly."]]]. Al-Nahhas said: The governing word of it cannot be "those who obstruct" nor "those who say," lest a separation be made between the *silah* (relative clause) and the *mawsul* (relative pronoun/antecedent). Ibn al-Anbari said: "Except a little" is incomplete, because "stingy" (*ashihhatan*) is linked to the first part, so it is in the accusative in four ways. One of them: you take it as a *qat'* (accusative of separation, in which a descriptive word is detached from its antecedent) from "those who obstruct," as if he said: Allah certainly knows those who obstruct others from fighting and who are stingy about spending on the poor Muslims. It may also be in the accusative as a *qat'* from "those who say," that is, while they are stingy. It may also be that you put it in the accusative as a *qat'* from what is in "they come," as if he said: "And they do not come to the battle except cowardly and stingy." It may also be that you put "stingy" in the accusative for *dhamm*. From this fourth analysis it is good to pause (*waqf*) at his words "except a little." "Stingy towards you" is a good pause (*waqf hasan*). Similar to it is "stingy towards the good" (*ashihhatan 'ala al-khayr*), which is a *hal* from the pronoun in "they lashed you" (*salaqukum*), and it is the governing word for it.

﴿So when fear comes, you see them looking to you, their eyes rolling like one fainting from death﴾. He described them with cowardice. Likewise is the way of the coward: he looks right and left with a fixed gaze, and he may faint. Regarding "fear" there are two views. One: fear of the enemy's fighting when it advances. This is said by al-Suddi. The second: fear of the Prophet ﷺ when he prevails. This is said by Ibn Shajarah. "You see them looking to you" is out of fear of fighting according to the first view, and out of fear of the Prophet ﷺ according to the second. "Their eyes rolling" is due to the loss of their reason, so that they cannot direct their gaze to any direction. It is also said: due to the intensity of their fear, fearing that death will come to them from every direction.

﴿But when fear departs, they lash you with sharp tongues﴾. Al-Farra' also reported *salaqukum* with the letter *sad* (ṣalaqukum). A *khatib* who is eloquent is called *musallaq* and *mislaq*. The root of *salq* is voice, and from it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "May Allah curse the woman who wails loudly, the woman who shaves her head, and the woman who tears her clothes." Al-A'sha said:

In them is glory and generosity, and nobility is in them, and the speaker is eloquent (*al-sallaq*) [[Also narrated as "*al-musallaq*."]].

Qatadah said: Its meaning is that they stretch out their tongues against you at the time of dividing the spoils, saying: "Give us, give us, for we have been present with you." So at the time of the spoils they are the most miserly of people and the most fluent of tongue, and at the time of battle they are the most cowardly of people and the most fearful. Al-Nahhas said: This is a good view, because after it comes "stingy towards the good" [[In the original sources: "stingy towards you."]]. It is also said: the meaning is that they exaggerated in disputing with you and arguing against you. Al-Qutabi said: The meaning is that they harmed you with harsh speech. *Al-salq* means harm. From it is the saying of the poet:

We have lashed Hawazin with Nawahil until we bowed low.

"Stingy towards the good": that is, towards the spoils. This is said by Yahya ibn Salam. It is also said: towards wealth, that they should spend it in the way of Allah. This is said by al-Suddi.

﴿Those have not believed﴾, meaning, not in their hearts, even if their outward appearance is belief. The hypocrite is a disbeliever in reality, because Allah the Mighty and Majestic described them with disbelief [[The wording of the original sources is: "If Allah the Mighty and Majestic had described them with disbelief," which is an error.]].

﴿So Allah has nullified their deeds﴾, meaning, He will not reward them for them, since they did not intend the Face of Allah the Exalted with them.

﴿And that is ever easy for Allah﴾. This may have two meanings: One: their hypocrisy was easy for Allah. The second: the nullifying of their deeds was easy for Allah.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 33, verse 20:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They think the confederates have not withdrawn﴾, meaning, out of their cowardice, they suppose the confederates have not dispersed, when in fact they had dispersed, but they had not gone far off on the march.

(And if the confederates should come) meaning, and if the confederates should return to them for fighting.

(They would wish that they were in the desert among the Bedouins) they would wish to be with the Bedouins, out of fear of being killed and waiting to see what befalls you. Talhah ibn Musarrif recited "law annahum budan fi al-a'rab" (they would wish that they were, in the desert, among the Bedouins). It is said: bad (بَادٍ, one dwelling in the desert) and budan (بُدًّى), like ghazin (غَازٍ) and ghuzzan (غُزًّى). It may also be pronounced with a long vowel, like sa'im (صَائِمٍ) and sawwam (صَوَّامٍ). Fulan badā yabdū (بَدَا فُلَانٌ يَبْدُو) means he went out into the desert, and it is al-bidawah and al-badawah (الْبِدَاوَةُ وَالْبَدَاوَةُ), with kasrah and fathah. The root of the word is from al-badw (البدو), which means appearance. "Yas'alun" (يَسْئَلُونَ). Ya'qub, in the transmission of Ruways, recited (yatasa'alūna 'an anba'ikum) (they ask one another about your news), meaning about the reports of the Prophet ﷺ. They say to one another: "Has Muhammad and his companions not been destroyed? Has Abu Sufyan and his confederates not prevailed?" That is, they would wish to be dwellers of the desert, asking about your news without witnessing the fighting, due to their extreme cowardice. It was also said: they are always, out of their cowardice, asking about the news of the believers and whether they have been struck. It was also said: among them, in the outskirts of Madinah, were those who had not attended the trench, and they began asking about your news and wishing for the defeat of the Muslims.

(And if they had been among you, they would not have fought except a little) meaning, shooting with arrows and stones out of showing off and seeking reputation. And if that had been for the sake of Allah, its little would have been much.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 33, verse 21:

There are two issues here. The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Verily, in the Messenger of Allah you have a good example﴾. This is a rebuke to those who stayed behind from fighting; that is, there was for you a model (qudwah) in the Prophet ﷺ, in that he gave himself for the support of the religion of Allah by going out to the Trench. Al-uswah is al-qudwah (model, example). 'Asim recited "uswah" with a damma on the hamza, while the rest recited it with a kasra, and both are dialects. According to al-Farra', the plural in both is the same. His reasoning for the damma, according to the dialect of those who use the kasra in the singular, is to distinguish between words of the waw type and words of the ya' type, so they say kiswah and kusan, and lihyah and luha. Al-Jawhari said: al-uswah and al-iswah, with damma and with kasra, are two dialects, and the plural is usan and isan. 'Uqbah ibn Hassan al-Hajari related from Malik ibn Anas, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, regarding "Verily, in the Messenger of Allah you have a good example," that he said: "In the hunger of the Prophet ﷺ." Al-Khatib Abu Bakr Ahmad mentioned it and said: 'Uqbah ibn Hassan alone transmitted it from Malik, and I have not written it except by this chain of narration.

The second: His saying, "uswah": al-uswah is al-qudwah. Al-uswah is that which one takes as a pattern, that is, that by which one is consoled. So one follows him in all his actions and is consoled by him in all his circumstances. His face was wounded, his front tooth was broken, his uncle Hamzah was killed, his belly was hungry, and he was found only patient, seeking reward, thankful and content. It is related from Anas ibn Malik, from Abu Talhah, who said: "We complained to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of hunger and lifted our stomaches [[addition from Sunan al-Tirmidhi]] from stone to stone, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ lifted his from two stones." Abu 'Isa al-Tirmidhi narrated it and said of it: "It is a gharib hadith." When his face was wounded he ﷺ said: "O Allah, forgive my people, for they do not know," and it has been mentioned before.

﴿For those who hope for Allah and the Last Day﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the meaning is: for whoever hopes to meet Allah, by his faith, and believes in the Resurrection in which actions are recompensed. It was also said: that is, for whoever hopes for the reward of Allah on the Last Day. According to the skilled grammarians, it is not permissible to write "yarjuwa" with an alif unless it is singular, because the reason that applies to the plural does not apply to the singular.

﴿And remembers Allah much﴾, out of fear of His punishment and hope for His reward. It was also said: "li-man" is a substitute (badal) for His saying "lakum," but the Basran grammarians do not permit this, because the absent (third person) cannot be substituted for the addressed (second person). Rather, the lam in "li-man" is connected to "hasanah," and "uswah" is the subject of "kana" and "lakum" is the predicate. Scholars differed about who is meant by this address, on two views: first, the hypocrites, by way of continuation of the address that preceded. Second, the believers, based on His saying, "for those who hope for Allah and the Last Day." Scholars also differed about whether this following of the Messenger, peace be upon him, is obligatory or recommended, on two views: first, it is obligatory until evidence shows it is recommended. Second, it is recommended until evidence shows it is obligatory. It is possible that it is understood as obligatory in matters of religion and as recommended in matters of worldly affairs.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 33, verse 22:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When the believers saw the confederates﴾. Some Arabs say "raʾā" (he saw) with metathesis (qalb), so that the form is "rāʾ". ﴿They said, "This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us."﴾ He means His saying, may He be exalted, in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿Or do you think that you will enter Paradise while there has not yet come to you the example of those who passed away before you?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:214], and the verse that follows. So when they saw the confederates on the day of the Trench, they said: "This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us." This is related from Qatadah.

A second opinion, transmitted by Kathir ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr al-Muzani from his father, from his grandfather, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) delivered a sermon in the year the confederates were mentioned, and said: "Jibril (peace be upon him) informed me that my community will prevail over it—that is, over the palaces of al-Hirah and the cities of Kisra—so rejoice in victory." The Muslims rejoiced and said: "Praise be to Allah, a true promise, since He promised us victory after siege." Then the confederates appeared, and the believers said: "This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us." This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

As for "mā waʿadanā": if you make "mā" mean "alladhī" (that which), then the returning pronoun (hāʾ) is omitted; if you make it a verbal noun (maṣdar), no returning pronoun is needed. ﴿And it increased them only in faith and submission.﴾ Al-Farra' said: "And the looking at the confederates increased them [in nothing] but..." Ali ibn Sulayman said: "raʾā" indicates seeing, and the feminine marking of "ruʾyah" (sight) is not real (ḥaqīqī), and the meaning is: the sight did not increase them except in faith in the Lord and submission to the decree; this was said by al-Hasan. And had he said "mā zādūhum" it would have been permissible.

When the matter grew severe for the Muslims and their stay in the Trench was prolonged, the Prophet (peace be upon him) stood on the mound on which the Mosque of Victory (Masjid al-Fath) stands, on one of the nights, awaiting what Allah had promised him of victory, and said: "Who will go to bring us news of them, and for him is Paradise?" No one answered him. He said it a second and a third time, and no one answered him. Then he looked to his side and said: "Who is this?" It was Hudhayfah. He said: "Did you not hear my words since tonight?" Hudhayfah said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, harm and cold prevented me from answering you.'" He said: "Go, until you enter among the people, listen to their speech, and bring me their news. O Allah, guard him from before him, from behind him, from his right and from his left, until you return him to me. Go, and do not do anything until you come to me." So Hudhayfah set off with his weapon, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) raised his hand, saying: "O helper of the distressed and O answerer of those in need, remove my worry, my grief and my distress, for You see my condition and the condition of my companions." Then Jibril descended and said: "Indeed Allah has heard your supplication and has sufficed you against the terror of your enemy." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fell prostrate on his knees, spread out his hands, and let his eyes flow, saying: "Thanks, thanks, as You have shown mercy to me and to my companions." Jibril informed him that Allah, may He be exalted, was sending a wind upon them, and he gave his companions the good news of this.

Hudhayfah said: "I reached them, and their fires were blazing. Then a violent wind came, carrying pebbles, and it left them no fire without extinguishing it and no tent without overturning it, and they began to shield themselves from the pebbles." Abu Sufyan got up to his mount and shouted to Quraysh: "Flee, flee!" Uyaynah ibn Hisn, al-Harith ibn ʿAwf and al-Aqraʿ ibn Habis did likewise. The confederates dispersed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rose in the morning and returned to Madinah with him in such disarray as Allah willed. Fatimah came to him with a washing solution and washed his head. Then Jibril came to him and said: "You have laid down the weapons, but the people of the heavens have not laid them down. I have continued to pursue them until I brought them to al-Rawha'"—then he said—"Rise up against Banu Qurayzah." Abu Sufyan said: "I kept hearing the clanging of weapons until I passed al-Rawha'."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 33, verses 23–24:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Among the believers are men﴾. *Rijal* (men) is in the nominative case, as the subject (*mubtada'*, the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence). The beginning of a sentence with an indefinite noun is permissible because *sadaqu* ("they were true") occupies the position of a qualifier (*na't*).

(﴿Among them is he who has fulfilled his vow﴾) *Min* ("among") is in the nominative position as a subject (*mubtada'*). Likewise ﴿and among them is he who awaits﴾, and the predicate (*khabar*, the complement of the subject) is in the prepositional phrase. *Al-nahb* means a vow or a pledge. One says from it: *nahabtu, ansahubu*, with a *damma*. The poet said:

*"And when Kalb vows upon the people, indeed they are more worthy of the crown of the noble, the generous one."*

Another said:

*"Glory has vowed upon us a vow [[Preceded by:*

*O Amr, O son of the most noble in lineage.]]"*

Another said:

*"Shall he vow and it is fulfilled, or [is it] error and falsehood? [[This is the second half of a line by Labid, whose first half is:*

*Do you not ask the man what he is striving for?]]"*

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Tirmidhi narrated from Anas, who said: My paternal uncle Anas ibn al-Nadr, after whom I was named, did not witness Badr with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it weighed heavily upon him. He said: "The first battle the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) attended, I was absent from it. By Allah, if Allah shows me a battle with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the future, Allah will surely see what I do." He said: So he was ashamed to say anything else, and he witnessed Uhud with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the following year. Sa'd ibn Malik met him and said: "O Abu 'Amr, where [are you going]?" He said: "Wahan [[This word is used to express admiration for something.]] for the scent of Paradise! I find it beyond Uhud." So he fought until he was killed, and there were found in his body eighty-some wounds, between a strike, a stab and an arrow. His paternal aunt al-Rubayyi' bint al-Nadr said: "I did not recognize my brother except by his fingertips." And this verse was revealed: ﴿Among the believers are men who have been true to what they pledged to Allah. Among them is he who has fulfilled his vow, and among them is he who awaits, and they have not changed in the least﴾. This is the wording of al-Tirmidhi, who said: This is a hadith *hasan sahih* (good and sound).

'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) said concerning His saying, ﴿Among the believers are men who have been true to what they pledged to Allah﴾, the verse: "Among them is Talhah ibn 'Ubaydullah, who stood firm with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) until his hand was struck." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Talhah has made Paradise obligatory [for himself] [[*Awjaba al-rajulu*: when a man does an action for which Paradise or Hellfire becomes due to him.]]."

In al-Tirmidhi, also from him: The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to a rustic ignorant Bedouin: "Ask him about the one who has fulfilled his vow, who is he?" They did not dare to ask him, out of reverence and awe for him. So the Bedouin asked him, and he turned away from him. Then he asked again, and he turned away from him. Then I looked from the door of the mosque, and I was wearing green garments. When the Prophet (ﷺ) saw me, he said: "Where is the one who asked about the one who has fulfilled his vow?" The Bedouin said: "I am here, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "This one is among those who have fulfilled their vow." He said: This is a hadith *hasan gharib* (good and strange), which we do not know except through the narration of Yunus ibn Bukayr.

Al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Hurayrah that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from Uhud, he passed by Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, who had been killed on the road. He stopped beside him and supplicated for him, then recited this verse: ﴿Among the believers are men who have been true to what they pledged to Allah. Among them is he who has fulfilled his vow﴾ up to ﴿and they have not changed in the least﴾. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I bear witness that these are martyrs before Allah on the Day of Resurrection. So visit them and greet them, for by Him in whose hand is my soul, no one will greet them until the Day of Resurrection except that they will return the greeting."

It was said: *al-nahb* means death, i.e., he died upon what he had pledged to, related from Ibn 'Abbas. *Al-nahb* also means a time or a period. It is said: "So-and-so has fulfilled his *nahb*" when he has died. Dhu al-Rummah said:

*"On an evening when the Harithis fled after he had fulfilled his *nahb* in the meeting-place of the horses, Hawbar."*

*Al-nahb* also means a need or an aspiration. One of them says: "I have no *nahb* with them," but this is not the intended meaning of the verse. The meaning of *nahb* in this place is a vow, as we mentioned earlier. That is: among them is he who exerted his effort in fulfilling his pledge until he was killed, like Hamzah, Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, Anas ibn al-Nadr and others. And among them is he who awaits martyrdom, and they did not change their pledge and vow.

It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he recited: "Among them is he who has fulfilled his vow, and among them is he who awaits, and among them is he who has changed [[*Badala*: to change.]] a change." Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: This hadith is rejected by the people of knowledge, because it contradicts the *ijma'* (scholarly consensus), and because it implies a slight upon the believers and the men whom Allah praised and honored with truthfulness and fidelity. No one among them is known to have changed, and none of their community is found to have altered, may Allah be pleased with them.

﴿That Allah may reward the truthful for their truthfulness﴾, i.e., Allah commanded jihad so that He may reward the truthful in the Hereafter for their truthfulness.

﴿And punish the hypocrites﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿if He wills﴾, i.e., if He wills to punish them, He does not grant them repentance; and if He does not will to punish them, He turns to them in repentance before death.

﴿Indeed Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 33, verse 25:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah turned back those who disbelieved, in their rage, not having obtained any good﴾. Muhammad ibn 'Amr traced it back (yarfa'uhu) to 'A'isha, who said: "Those who disbelieved" here refers to Abu Sufyan and 'Uyayna ibn Badr. Abu Sufyan returned to Tihama, and 'Uyayna returned to Najd.

(And Allah sufficed the believers in the fighting) by sending against them a wind and hosts, until they returned, and the Banu Qurayza returned to their fortresses (sayasi, sing. saysa), so the affair of Qurayza was settled by terror (bi-l-ru'b).

(And Allah is ever Strong) in His command (Mighty) who cannot be overcome.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 33, verse 26–27:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He brought down those of the People of the Book who supported them from their fortresses﴾. He means those who aided the confederates (al-Ahzab): Quraysh and Ghatafan, and they are Banu Qurayzah. Their story has already passed. (From their fortresses) means from their strongholds, the singular of which is ṣayṣah (fortress, stronghold).

The poet said:

"So the oxen became slain, and the women of Tamim became
Gathering up the horns (ṣayāṣiyā)."

[The verse is by ʿAbd Banī al-Ḥasḥās, and Ṣāḥib al-Lisān cited it as evidence that ṣayāṣī of cattle means their horns. Its version of the line is:

"So the oxen became drowned, and the women of Tamim became
Gathering up the horns (al-ṣayāṣiyā)."

That is, they gathered up the horns to weave with them. He means that because of the abundance of rain, the wild beasts drowned.]

From this word comes the name given to the weaver's spike with which he arranges the warp and the weft: ṣayṣah. Durayd ibn al-Ṣimmah said:

"I came to him while the spears were tearing at him,
Like the striking of the ṣayāṣī on the stretched weave."

From it also comes ṣayṣat al-dik (the spur of the rooster), which is on its leg. The ṣayāṣī of cattle are their horns, because they defend themselves with them. Sometimes they were fitted onto spears in place of spearheads. It is said: "May God cut off his ṣayṣiyah," meaning his root.

(And He cast terror into their hearts; a group you killed) and they are the men.

(And a group you took captive) and they are the women and the offspring, as has been mentioned previously.

(And He caused you to inherit their land, their homes, their wealth, and a land you had not trodden) yet. Yazid ibn Ruman, Ibn Zayd and Muqatil said: it means Hunayn, and they had not yet attained it, so God promised them it. Qatadah said: "We used to hear that it is Makkah." Al-Hasan said: it is Persia and Rome. ʿIkrimah said: every land conquered until the Day of Resurrection.

(And God is over all things Competent) has two interpretations. The first: He is Competent over whatever He wills for His servants, whether punishment or pardon; this was said by Muhammad ibn Ishaq. The second: He is Competent over what He wills to conquer of fortresses and villages; this was said by al-Naqqash. It has also been said: (And God is over all things) of what He promised you (Competent), whose power is not repelled and to whom incapacity is not attributed, exalted is He. It is said: tasirūna and tasurūna (with the sin kasrah and dammah), related by al-Farra'.
